After the kings were expelled, the consulship was the highest of these offices. Next came the dignity of the legate, because what the consul undertook to do, his legate carried out. Just as the kings wore a crown on their heads.

or a diadem. Likewise, the consuls bore fasces instead, at the head [?] (in capite). Those were the insignia of majesty (insignia maiestatis), that is, the ornaments and tokens of supreme power. Just as in a house we call the greatest pillar the "main pillar" (I mean the one that bears the roof-ridge), so the power of the consuls, or of the kings, or of the dictators was called "main power" (majesty), because it was the greatest. Those who were disobedient to the majesty of the kings or of the consuls, and were condemned for it before them, had recourse to the people according to Roman law, so that the people might help them out of their peril. That recourse was called provocatio (appeal). But since very great dissensions often arose from this, the Romans appointed a dictator to put an end to the dissensions, and his majesty was such

that no one could appeal to the people (provocatio ad populum) against what was adjudged against him before the dictator. A master of soldiers (magister militum) always attended him, and the dictator chose him himself, just as the consul chose his legate. After them came the tribunes of the plebs, who were very powerful. Sometimes there were two of them, sometimes even ten, and they were often created in such a way that they had consular power, that is, power similar to the consuls'. They were called tribunes of the plebs because they took the judgments of the plebs upon themselves. After them came the praetors, the censors and the quaestors. The praetors went before the consul in the army and set up his praetorium for him, I mean his tent, in which he sat to judge and to address assemblies (ad iudicandum et contionandum), that is, to judge and to speak.

From this he was called praetor, from praeeundo (going before), as if "praeitor". The censors controlled the public treasury, which was kept in the aerarium; therefore they were called censors, from census. The quaestors were the collectors of the treasury, so called as if "quaesitores" (seekers). After them came the prefects, that is, overseers, who were in charge of various affairs. Then there were the aediles, who guarded the buildings (aedes) and inspected them. Those who sat in judgment over crimes were called duumvirs and triumvirs. For this reason Suetonius charges Augustus with having been most severe in his triumvirate. Later, governors (praesides) replaced the duumvirs and triumvirs. The decemvirate was established only once, when the Romans chose ten men instead of two consuls, so that they bore the fasces one at a time and each in turn cared earnestly for the commonwealth. Proconsuls served in place of the consuls. The pontiffs took care of religion.
Emperors, dukes and counts are well known.

ON THE ORDER OF ROMAN CITIZENS. It is also useful to know that Roman citizens were divided into the fathers (patres) and the plebs. Among the fathers there were three orders. The highest order was that of the clarissimi (most distinguished). Hence we read in the Passion of Saint Sebastian: "Every day he urged the most distinguished men Marcellian and Mark to reject the blandishments of the world." The second was that of the illustres (illustrious). Boethius belonged to it. Therefore the title of this book says: "Of Anicius Manlius Severinus, an illustrious man." The third was that of the spectabiles (notable), as blessed Agatha said of herself: "I am freeborn, and of a notable family." Among the plebs there were two orders.

equestrian and pedestrian. A man was an eques (knight) if he could produce ten thousand of the heavy coins that were called sestertia. Those who had less had to go on foot. When it was time to appoint officials, the patres appointed them per suffragia plebis (by the votes of the people). The people's consent and their requests were what was called suffragia. Those who had come there from other cities had the same law, except that they could not ferre suffragia (cast votes). From this it is clear that those who were called patres and senators had great dignitas (rank and honour) even without holding office.
LIKEWISE. For as we said a little before, what has no beauty of its own now gains splendour through the opinion of those who make use of it,
and now loses it. As I rightly said before, high rank, which has no beauty of its own, gains it and loses it according to what the people who hold it think.

CONCLUSION. If, therefore, high offices cannot make men worthy of reverence (suspension); if, moreover, they are soiled by contact with the wicked (and this); if they stop shining when times change (and this); if they become cheap in the opinion of nations (and this): what beauty worth seeking do they have in themselves, let alone (nedum, that is, 'not to say') beauty they could give to others? Resolution. If lordships cannot make men honourable, if even the wickedness of worthless men disgraces them, and if they fade with age,
that is, come to stand [?] (slíngen), and if they are despised by distant peoples, what desirable beauty do they then have in them? I need not ask what of it they could give to others.

LIKEWISE. Although Nero of raging luxury (that is, full of cruelty and luxury) proudly adorned himself with Tyrian purple and snow-white gems. Though the cruel and very lustful Nero proudly decked himself out with the costliest purple and with beautiful gems, yet he flourished hated by all. He was always hateful to all his people, not venerable. Yet the wicked man once gave unseemly curule chairs to the venerable fathers. Wicked as he was, he still bestowed unseemly offices on the venerable lords. Unseemly, because they came from a wicked hand.
Who, then, would think those honours blessed
which wretched men bestow? Who, then, will think that honours given by the wretched are blessed? An argument from contraries, as blessedness and miseries are.
THIRD, ON POWERS. Or can kingdoms and closeness to kings make a man powerful?

Can the power of kings, and being on intimate terms with them, make men mighty? Why not? "Why can it not?" you say. When their good fortune lasts forever? Since no one pushes kings down, and their good fortune stays with them? Yet antiquity is full of examples, and so is the present age, of kings who exchanged good fortune for calamity. We have many examples of this, from old times and from new, of how many kings came from good fortune to misery.
O glorious power, which is found not strong enough even to preserve itself! This is truly a famous power, which cannot even keep itself. But if this power of kingdoms

…is the author of blessedness, would it not, if it were lacking in any part, diminish happiness and bring in misery? If the power of kings creates blessedness, where is it then, since it must follow that wherever that power fails, the failing diminishes the blessedness and brings in wretchedness? But however widely human empires extend,
many peoples must still be left over whom any given king does not rule.

Even if earthly kingdoms extend far, there are still always many peoples over whom a king, however powerful, does not rule. But in whatever part the power that makes people blessed ceases, powerlessness, which makes them wretched, creeps in. Where the power that makes people blessed leaves off, the powerlessness that makes them wretched comes in. This is an argument from contraries. In this way, therefore, kings must have the greater share of misery. In this way it is necessary, that is, from this it follows necessarily, that more wretchedness than blessedness lies upon kings.
A tyrant who had learned the dangers of his lot, that is, of his high rank, depicted the fears of kingship by the terror of a sword hanging above the head. Dionysius, who ruled Sicily tyrannically,

and therefore knew the perils of his power, compared the fears he suffered on account of his kingdom to the fear of a sword hanging above one's head. He hung it by a thin thread over the head of a man who had told him that he was blessed, and asked him: "How blessed are you now?" "How can I be blessed," he said, "while I fear this sword?" "I am just as blessed," said Dionysius, "fearing the same thing." What then is this power, which cannot drive away the bites of cares and cannot escape the stings of fears? What sort of power can that be, which cannot keep a man from being bitten by cares and goaded by fears?
Yet they themselves would wish to have lived secure,

but they cannot. Now they would gladly live securely, but they cannot. Then they boast of their power. And yet they boast of their power. Do you consider a man powerful whom you see wishing for what he cannot bring about? Do you consider a man powerful who cannot do what he wishes? Do you consider a man powerful who surrounds himself with a bodyguard? Do you consider a man blessed who always surrounds his side with servants? Who himself fears those whom he terrifies more than they fear him? Who fears those whom he threatens?
Who, in order to seem powerful, depends on the hands of those who serve him? In whose men's hands it lies
whether he is powerful. For why should I discuss the intimates of kings, when I show that kingdoms themselves are full of such great weakness?

What need is there for me to speak of the intimates of kings and how weak they are, since I have shown the kings themselves to be so weak? Royal power often brings them down, sometimes while it stands unharmed, sometimes after it has fallen. The power of kings overthrows them, sometimes while it stands upright, sometimes when it falls. When the king falls, his intimates fall; often he himself also brings them down. So they are even weaker. Nero forced Seneca, his intimate friend and teacher, to choose the manner of his own death.

This can be seen in how Nero drove his intimate and his teacher Seneca to choose his own death. When Nero wanted him dead, he presented it to him as a kind of honour, letting him choose his manner of death. After that he brought in the physician, who let his blood in the bath until Seneca grew so weak that he died of it. Antoninus threw Papinian, long powerful among the courtiers, to the soldiers' swords. That is, Antoninus, surnamed Pius, the twelfth emperor after Augustus, ordered his soldiers to kill Papinian, who had long held power there at court. And yet both of them wished to give up their power. Both of them would gladly have rid themselves of their power while they were still safe.
Of these, Seneca even tried to hand over his wealth to Nero

and to withdraw into retirement. Seneca was even willing to give all his property to Nero and live quietly at home. But while their very weight drags down those who are about to fall, neither achieved what he wanted. As it always goes, their burden pulls down those who are sinking, so neither of them escaped, and neither got what he wanted. They were overloaded, and that brought them down. What then is this power that frightens those who have it? What kind of power is it, then,
that those who have it fear? A power that leaves you unsafe while you choose to keep it, and that you cannot escape when you want to lay it down?

A power that leaves you unsafe while you have it, if you want to keep it, and that you cannot [get away] from if you do not want it? Or are friends a protection when fortune, not virtue, has won them? Will friends help keep you safe, when most of them come to you through good fortune rather than through virtue? But someone whom good fortune made a friend, misfortune will make an enemy. So do not trust them, because a person good fortune made a friend, misfortune soon makes an enemy.
And what plague does more harm than an enemy in one's own household? What sickness is more harmful than an enemy who is close to you?
WHAT TRUE POWER IS. Whoever wants to be powerful
must tame his fierce passions
and not bow his neck, conquered by lust,

to shameful reins. Whoever wants to be powerful must subdue his wanton mind, and must not let his neck be conquered by desire and made subject to its shameful bridle. That is, he must not give in to his desires.
For though the far-off land of India may tremble at your laws
and distant Thule may serve you. For even if the most remote lands fear your power, such as India in the east and Thule in the north,
still, to be unable to drive away black cares
and to banish miserable complaints
is not power. If you can never overcome harmful cravings and wretched complaints, that is, the sins that deserve lament, that is powerlessness, and it makes you powerless.

FOURTH, ON GLORY. But glory: how deceptive it often is, how shameful! But glory, how false it often is, and how shameful. It is shameful because it is false. Therefore the tragic poet rightly exclaims:

So the tragic poet among the Greeks can boldly cry: 'Glory, glory, for thousands of mortals you have become nothing but a great puffing-up of the ears.' (Greek, partly garbled: O doxa doxa myrioisi de broton … oden gagosen ei oton oggosas megan [?].) Yes: glory, glory, for a thousand people you have become nothing but a great swelling of the ears. The ears like to hear praise, and so they open themselves to it.

For many have often carried off a great name because of the false opinions of the crowd. Many have often won a great name from the false reputation they have among the people. What could be thought of that is more shameful than this? What then can be more worthless, or be imagined? For those who are falsely praised
must themselves blush at their own praises.

Those who are praised wrongly cannot help being ashamed of their praise. But even if that praise has been earned by merit, what will it have added to the wise man's conscience? Even if a good reputation is won rightly, what more virtue does the wise man then know himself to have? He measures his good not by popular rumour but by the truth of his conscience. He does not judge his worth by reputation, but by the truth his conscience knows.
But if it seems a fine thing to have spread this name widely,

it follows that he should not be judged to have spread a shameful one. If a man thinks it a fine thing to have spread his name widely, then it is fitting that people should not think he is spreading a shameful name, but a truly glorious one. But since, as I explained a little earlier, there must be many peoples whom one man's fame cannot reach,
it happens that the man you consider glorious seems inglorious in the nearest part of the world.

But since, as I said before, there must be many peoples whom one man's reputation cannot fully reach, it follows that the man you consider glorious is unregarded in another land. Among these things, I do not even think popular favour worth mentioning. So I do not consider the people's praise worth my even mentioning it. It does not come from judgement, and it never lasts firmly. It does not come from any careful judgement at all, and it does not hold firm.

ITEM. Now who does not see how empty and how futile the name of nobility is? The name of noble birth, which many take pride in: how vain and how contemptible is it? "Futile" is the word for a leaky vessel that has cracked open

or has become useless. A man who is worthless in himself and still wants to be called a nobleman is like such a vessel. If nobility is counted as renown, that renown belongs to someone else. That name should therefore not be counted as fame for him, because it belongs to another. For nobility seems to be a kind of praise that comes from the merits of one's parents. As this definition shows, nobility is praise that has come down from the worth of one's ancestors.
But if being proclaimed is what makes a person renowned, then the people who must be renowned are the ones being proclaimed.

Since praise makes people famous, the ancestors whose praise it is are the famous ones. So another person's renown does not make you illustrious if you have none of your own. Another person's fame does not make you illustrious if you have none of your own. But if there is anything good in noble birth, I think it is only this: that the noble seem to be placed under an obligation not to fall short of their ancestors' virtue. If there is anything good in noble birth, I consider this one thing alone to be good: that the nobly born feel obliged to take after their ancestors in virtue.
THAT ALL HAVE ONE ORIGIN. The whole race of men on earth springs from a like birth. From a like origin all people on earth have come.
For there is one father of things; one provides for all. Of all creatures there is one father; one cares for them all.
He gave rays to Phoebus and gave horns to the moon. He made the sun shine and the moon horned.
He also gave men to the earth and stars to the sky. He created men on earth and stars in heaven.
He enclosed in limbs the souls sought from the lofty seat. He shut the soul within the limbs, sent down here from heaven.
Therefore a noble seed brings forth all mortals. Therefore a noble seed has brought forth all men, because they are born from heaven.
Why do you clamour about lineage and ancestors? Why then do you boast of your kin and your forefathers? If your beginnings…
…and God your author you consider, no one stands out as degenerate.

If you look to the beginning and to God the creator, then no one is ignoble, unless, cherishing worse things through vices, he forsakes his own origin. Unless he chooses by sinning to renounce his origin: if he forsakes his creator, then he becomes ignoble.

THE FIFTH [GOOD SOUGHT] IS IN PLEASURE. But what shall I say of the pleasures of the body? What can I say about the body's delights? The craving for them is full of anxiety, and their fulfilment full of regret.

[?] which cause a man great distress while he craves them, and which he grows just as weary of once they are fulfilled? How many diseases, how unbearable the pains they usually bring upon the bodies of those who enjoy them, as a kind of fruit of wickedness! How many sicknesses, how severe the pains it gives to those given to it, as if as interest on the wickedness! Therefore a poet said: "For in one and the same way wine and Venus do harm." What pleasantness their stirrings hold, I do not know. What delight there may be in their craving, I do not know. How can it be delight when it is anxiety?
But anyone who is willing to recall his own lusts will understand that the outcome of pleasures is sad.

But how sorrowful the outcome is, he will recognize who is willing to remember his lusts. If these can make men blessed, there is no reason why cattle too should not be called blessed. If they can make men happy, then nothing prevents the beast from being happy as well. Their whole aim hurries toward filling the bodily void. Its whole mind is set on filling the belly [literally, the tub].
LIKEWISE. Most honourable indeed would be the delight of a wife and children, but it has been said all too truly to nature that someone or other found his children to be his tormentors.

I would say that wife and children were chaste joys, except that it is said (which is far outside nature) that some children or other were the tormentors of their father. How biting any condition of theirs is, I need not remind you, who have learned it by experience elsewhere and are anxious now. However chaste their nature may be, I still need not remind you how full of care it is, since you have learned it elsewhere and are always anxious about your own children.

In this I approve the opinion of my Euripides, who said that a man without children is happy in his misfortune. For this reason I praise the saying of my dear Euripides, a Greek poet and philosopher, who said that the childless man is happy through his misfortune.
LIKEWISE. Every pleasure has this:
it drives the frenzied on with goads. All pleasures have this in common: they goad the eager and drive them on to the deed.
And like the flying bees. And they are like the bees.
When it has poured out its pleasing honey
it flees. That is, when pleasure has completed its sweetness, it shudders at what it has done. When pleasure has done the deed, it then makes it loathsome.
And it strikes the hearts it has wounded with a bite that clings too tightly.

And then it bites the hurt heart with a bite that holds fast. This is what happens to the bee: when it stings in revenge it loses its sting, and then it flees in fear because it has no defence. After that it is called fucus (a drone), that is, one that eats the honeycomb but does not make it.

HE RECAPITULATES THE FIVE ABOVE. There is therefore no doubt that these ways to happiness are certain byways. Since this is so, there is no doubt that these five ways lead away from the path to happiness,

nor can they bring anyone to the place to which they promise to bring him. Nor can they lead anyone all the way to where they promise. But I will show very briefly with how many evils they are entangled. How many evils are in those things that take away happiness, I said before at length; now I will sum it up briefly.
RICHES. What then? Will you try to gather money? But you will snatch it from someone who has it. What do you desire? Do you desire to gather treasure? Then you take it from another.
HONOURS. Would you shine in high offices? You will have to beg the one who grants them. Would you shine in office? Then you must plead with the one who gives it.
And you who long to go ahead of others in honour become cheap through the humility of asking. And by begging you become more despised than the others whom you long to rank above.
POWER. Do you desire power? Exposed to the plots of your subjects, you will lie open to dangers. Would you become powerful? Then your own people will lie in wait for you, and so you are in peril.

FAME. Do you seek glory? But dragged in different directions through every kind of hardship, you are no longer secure. Do you long for renown? Then you must live in anxiety, entangled in the troublesome affairs by which you wish to win glory.
PLEASURE. Do you choose a life of pleasure? Would you live a life of pleasure?
But who would not scorn and throw away being a slave of the body, a most worthless and most fragile thing?

Whom should it not shame to be the servant of the body, the most despised and the frailest of things? Those who serve pleasure are the servants of the body. Those who serve the spirit are spiritual and like God, who is spirit, and therefore they are free.

THAT IN THE GOODS OF THE BODY MEN ARE NOT EQUAL TO THE BEASTS. Now those who carry the goods of the body before them: how slight and how fragile a possession they rely on! Those who put the goods of the body before the goods of the soul rely on a very small thing. The phrase "carry before them" is taken from the simiae, which we call apes. The ape always bears two young, and of the two

one is dearer to it than the other. It always carries the dearer one in front of it, and the other follows it. When people start to hunt it, it lifts the dearer one up to its breast. The less loved one jumps up onto its back and holds on by its hair. When it is then hard pressed, it lets go of the dearer one and escapes with the one it loved less. Can you surpass elephants in bulk, or bulls in strength? Can you become bigger than elephants, or stronger than bulls? Will you outrun tigers in speed? Or be swifter than tigers? "Tigris" means "arrow." The animal has that name from its swiftness, because no one can escape it. Saint Ambrose writes about this in the Hexameron.

Whoever steals its young from it while it is out hunting does not trust that he can escape it, and so he has provided himself with glass balls. Where it overtakes him, he throws one of them to it, as if he were giving the young one back to it. In the ball it sees itself and thinks the image is its young, and busies itself with suckling it. When it has no success at this and runs after him again, he deceives it with the second ball, and with the third, and so on, until he saves himself. Look at the expanse of the heavens, their firmness, their swiftness, and stop at last admiring worthless things. Consider how great the heavens are compared with elephants, how firm and strong compared with bulls, how swift compared with tigers, and let worthless things not be a wonder to you. Since the earth is great

and yet bears no comparison with the heavens, who then can know their breadth and their greatness? Since, wide as they are, they still turn round in twenty-four hours, what then can be so swift and so quick? Since even that immeasurable speed does not break them apart, what then is so firm? Yet the heavens are not to be admired for these things so much as for the reason by which they are governed. They are not so wonderful for the three things named as for the reason that drives them. That reason is God's wisdom. But the splendor of beauty: how swift it is, how fleeting, more fleeting than the changeableness of spring flowers! Consider also how hastily and how quickly it passes for you, the beauty of a man's appearance (I mean of his form), and how it is more changeable than the beauty of flowers.

But if, as Aristotle says, people had the eyes of a lynx. If people had lynx eyes, as Aristotle says. So that their sight could pass through what stands in its way. I mean that they could see right through a person. Once the insides were seen, would not the body of Alcibiades, most beautiful on the surface, seem utterly ugly? If they saw inside, would not even the body of Alcibiades seem badly made to them? He had the most beautiful body of all on the outside. We do not know who the beautiful Alcibias was, though many guess that she was the mother of Hercules, because he was called Alcides.
So it is not your nature that makes you seem beautiful, but the weakness of the eyes that look at you.

Your nature does not make you seem beautiful to people, because inside you are dung. The weakness of the eyes does that. But value the goods of the body as highly as you like, while knowing that whatever you admire can be destroyed by the small fire of a three-day fever. Now prize the body however you wish, though you know that what is so wonderfully precious to you can die of a three-day fever.
From all this we may sum it up, that is, put it briefly. From all these words I will bring it down to the shortest form. These things cannot provide the goods they promise,

and they are not perfect by bringing all goods together, so they do not lead to happiness like paths, nor do they themselves make people happy. The five things cannot bring what they promise, and they are not perfect through the union of all good,

so they are not ways to happiness and do not make people happy. The perfect gathering together of all goods is happiness. Where that is lacking, there is no happiness. So this argument is called 'from the cause,' that is, from the efficient cause. How can the effect be present where the efficient cause is not? Sometimes she teaches him to infer the cause from the end, and sometimes the end from the cause. Just as cause and efficient cause are one, so end, effect and outcome are also all one. With these two topics of argument, and also with clear examples, she has taught us along with Boethius that happiness is not found in the five things. All disputations get their strength from arguments and from syllogisms,

and from definitions, and also from the examples of the ancients and from divine authority. What else could one use to strengthen them? Even so, what syllogistic reasoning shows us is more certain than what arguments show, because some arguments are probable, that is, believable: they can sometimes be true and sometimes false. Others are necessary, that is, true of necessity. But syllogisms never deceive, if they are properly constructed. So she has saved them for later, for a stronger disputation.
LAMENT OVER HUMAN BLINDNESS. Alas, what ignorance leads the wretched astray down a pathless track! Ah, how grievously! What ignorance misleads you wretched people and leads you so far off the road?
You do not look for gold in a green tree,
nor do you pick gems from the vine. Indeed, you do not think of looking for gold on trees, or of breaking gems off vines.
You do not hide snares on high mountains,
so that you may enrich your feasts with fish. Indeed, you do not set your nets on the mountains to fish.
Nor, if it pleases you to hunt roe deer,
you search the Tyrrhenian shallows, that is, the Tuscan Sea.
Nor, on the other hand, if you want to hunt, do you encircle the sea-waves. Moreover, they know the very recesses, that is, the secret places of the sea,
hidden by the waves.
which water is more fruitful in snow-white gems, that is, in large pearls,

or which in red purple, that is, in the purple-shellfish. They know well the familiar places of the sea: which are rich in the white large pearls, which we call pearls, and which in purple, that is, the blood of the purple-shellfish.
And also which shores yield tender fish

or rough sea urchins. And which shores are rich in tender fish, or in the rough echini. The echinus is a small, sweet fish, as rough as a hedgehog. Its nature is such that if it begins to cling to a ship, no storm comes great enough to move the ship.
But where the good that they desire lies hidden,
blind, they put up with not knowing. But where the good is that they go about seeking, that they do not want to know.
And what has gone beyond the star-bearing pole
they seek, sunk in the earth. And what has passed beyond heaven, they want to dig up out of the earth.
What fitting curse shall I call down on such foolish minds? What may I now rightly pray for on behalf of such foolish minds?
Let them strive after wealth and honors,
and when they have gained false goods with heavy burden,

then let them recognize the true ones. This is what I will wish for them: since they will not turn back, let them go after honors and after riches, which are false goods, and when they become aware of the burden, may God grant them by it that they recognize the true goods. This I wish for them; this I pray for them.
WHAT LEADS THE FOLLOWERS OF FALSE HAPPINESS ASTRAY.
Let it be enough to have shown the form of false happiness up to this point. Now let the image of false happiness be enough to have shown you.
If you see it clearly, the next step is to show what the true one is. If you understand it well, then it is time for me to show you the true one. "Yet," I said,

"I see that neither can sufficiency be gained through wealth, nor power through kingdoms, nor reverence through offices, nor renown through glory, nor gladness through pleasures." "I see well," I said, "that one gains neither sufficiency through wealth, nor power through a kingdom, nor honor through office, nor renown through glory, nor joy through pleasure."
"Have you also grasped the reasons why this is so?" "Can you tell," she said, "what that means?"

"I seem to see it, though only as through a narrow crack." "It seems to me," I said, "that I see it as through a narrow slit." "But I would rather learn it more plainly from you." "I would gladly understand it more plainly from you." "Yet the reason is very easy to see." "Truly," she said, "it is a plain explanation."
"For what is simple and undivided by nature, human error separates." Now hear it: what is truly simple by nature

and undivided, people's error tries to divide. "And it carries it over from the true and perfect to the false and imperfect." And it leads it away from the true and the perfect to the false and the imperfect.

[Rubric:] Where one is, none of these five is lacking. Or do you think that what lacks nothing is in need of power? Do you think that what is in need of nothing could be in need of power? By no means, I said. No, I said. If it is in need of nothing, how can it then be in need of any single thing?
That is written in the Peri Hermeneias: if a universal negative is true, then the particular affirmative is false. You are right indeed. In that you are right, she said. For if there is anything
that has weaker strength in any matter, in that matter it must need the help of another.

Whatever is powerless in anything, in that it needs the help of another. That is called an argument from adjuncts: weakness is always joined with the need for help. So it is, I said. That is so, I said. Therefore sufficiency and power have one and the same nature. Since it is so, she said, sufficiency and power are one nature. So it seems. So it must be, I said. That too is from adjuncts.
Likewise. But what is of this kind, do you think it should be despised, or, on the contrary, that it is the most worthy of all things of veneration?

That in which sufficiency and power are, she said, is it contemptible, or worthy of all honours? But this, I said, cannot even be doubted. There can be no doubt about it, I said, except that the third follows from those two. Let us therefore add reverence to sufficiency and power, so that we judge these three to be one. Now let us put together, she said, sufficiency and power and reverence, so that we hold the three as one. Let us add it, if indeed we wish to confess the truth. Let us do so, I said, as we ought, if we wish to admit what is true.
Likewise. But what, she said, do you think this is obscure and ignoble, or most illustrious with all renown?

That in which those three are, she said, do you think it is without renown and ignoble, or the most renowned of all things? But consider whether what has been granted to lack nothing, to be most powerful, and to be most worthy of honour, would lack renown, which it could not supply for itself, and for that reason seem in some part more contemptible. Consider this for yourself: whether what is without need of anything, and mighty, and honourable, as you have admitted, could be without need and yet not be renowned [?], and whether for that reason it would be somewhat more contemptible than the others. I cannot, I said, but confess that this, as it is,
so too is most renowned.

I cannot admit anything else about it, I said, except what is so: that it is necessarily renowned. It follows, then, that we must admit that renown differs in nothing from the three above. If this is so, she said, then we must also admit that renown is not separate from the three above. It follows, I said. It is not separate, I said.

LIKEWISE. That which needs nothing outside itself, which can do all things by its own powers, and which is famous and revered: is it not clear that this is also the most joyful? "That which is without need of anything else," she said, "which is capable by its own strength, which is famous

and worthy of honour, is that not also the most joyful of all things?" "But I cannot even imagine," I said, "from where any sorrow could creep in on such a thing." "I could never conceive," I said, "from where sadness could come to such a thing." "So it is full of joy, if indeed the earlier points stand:

that must be admitted." "Therefore it must be admitted, if the earlier reckoning is true, that it is full of joy." "And by the same reasoning it is also necessary that the names of sufficiency, power, fame, reverence, and pleasure are different, but that their substance does not differ at all." "Therefore it is necessary," she said, "that the five have different names and yet are one being." "It is necessary," I said. "Truly necessary," I said. She has worked through all five with the same single argument she began with. That is the argument "from adjuncts" (ab adiunctis). Each of them is joined to the others, and therefore no one can separate them.

ON THE VARIOUS CHOICES OF THE GOOD. "So this, which is one and simple by nature, human depravity divides." Now you have heard that human wrongdoing strives to split what is one by nature and is simple.

"And while it tries to obtain a part of a thing that has no parts, it gets neither the portion, which does not exist, nor the thing itself, which it does not seek at all." And by seeking a part of that

which is undivided, they miss the very thing that they ought to seek, and yet do not seek. "In what way?" I said. In what manner? said I. "He who seeks riches," she said, "to escape poverty, takes no trouble over power; he would rather be lowly and obscure." He who strives for wealth while fleeing want does not ask for power; he would rather be despised and unknown. "He also denies himself many pleasures, even natural ones, so as not to lose the money he has gathered." And he takes from himself many of his comforts, even natural ones such as sleep, so that he may keep the treasure he has won.
"But in this way not even sufficiency comes to the one whom strength deserts,

whom trouble stings, whom lowliness casts down, whom obscurity hides." But someone who acts this way loses even sufficiency, since he loses even power. Discomfort stings him, contempt makes him an outcast, and obscurity keeps him hidden. Because he wants to have one thing without the others, which are its adjuncts, he loses that too.
LIKEWISE. "But he who desires only power squanders wealth, despises pleasures,
and counts honour without power, and glory as well, as worth nothing."

He who loves power alone drives away his wealth and cares neither for pleasures, nor for honours without power, nor for glory. "But you see how much this man lacks as well." There you also see what he lacks. "For it happens that sometimes he lacks necessities, that he is gnawed by anxieties." It often happens that he goes without his necessities and that anxieties goad him.
And since he cannot drive these things away, even in what he most sought
he ceases to be powerful. And so it happens to him that, since he cannot defend himself against this, the power that was all he wanted also slips away from him.
LIKEWISE. "One may reason in the same way about honours, glory and pleasures." I can say the same about honours,
glory and pleasures. "For since each of these is the same as the others, whoever seeks any one of them without the others
does not grasp even what he desires." Since they are one, he who desires one of them without the others does not get even that one.
LIKEWISE. "What then," I said, "if someone should wish to obtain all of them at once?" But what, said I, about someone who wants to gain all five together?
He would indeed wish for the summit of happiness. That is the one, she said, who wishes to gain the whole of happiness. But will he find it in these things,
which we have shown cannot give what they promise?

But do you think he would find it in the things that I have shown you cannot do what they promise? By no means, I said. No, said I. Therefore happiness is in no way to be sought in these things, each of which is believed to supply some of the things to be desired. So, she said, happiness is not to be sought in those five things, each of which can give something that people desire, but not everything. I admit it, I said. That is so, said I. And nothing truer than this can be said. And nothing is truer than this, of all that one can say.
"So you have," she said, "both the form of false happiness and its causes."
"Now," she said, "you have the image of false happiness, and with it the reason why it is false. It would not be false if people did not hasten to separate things that are inseparable."

HE URGES ONE WHO IS ALREADY TURNING AWAY FROM FALSE HAPPINESS TO DIRECT HIMSELF TOWARD THE TRUE. Now turn the gaze of your mind to the opposite side. Now look over there, toward what is opposite to it. For there you will at once see the true happiness that we promised. There you will see straight away the true one that I promised to show you. "But this," I said, "is clear even to a blind man."

"Truly," I said, "even a blind man can see it. And you showed it a little earlier, while you were trying to reveal the causes of the false one. You showed it there, when you showed where the falsehood comes from. For unless I am mistaken, true and perfect happiness is the kind that makes a person self-sufficient ...

powerful, worthy of reverence, renowned, and joyful. Unless my opinion deceives me, the true happiness is the one that makes a man rich, mighty, honorable, famous, and glad. And so that you may know that I have understood this inwardly: whatever can truly provide one of these,
since they are all the same thing, I recognize without any doubt that this is full happiness.

And so that you know my inner mind on this: whatever can truly give one of the five, since they are all one, I acknowledge to be full happiness." "O my pupil, I count you happy in this opinion," she said, "if indeed you add this." "God has looked kindly on you for this opinion, my dear one," she said, "if you add this to complete it."

"What is that?" I said. "Which one?" I said. "Do you think there is anything in these mortal and perishable things that can bring about a state of this kind?" "I am bringing you to this," she said. "Do you think there is anything in these short-lived worldly things that can give a person this state? That is what I wanted you to add." "By no means do I think so," I said.
"and you have shown this so fully that nothing more is needed."

"No, I do not think so," I said. "You have taught me this so well that there is no need for more." "Therefore these things seem to give mortals either images of the true good or certain imperfect goods." "They can give a person," she said, "what looks like the good, or what is imperfect good. But they cannot give the true and perfect good." "I agree," I said.

"I grant that," I said. "Since, then, you have recognized which happiness is the true one, and which ones falsely imitate it, it now remains for you to learn where you can seek this true one." "Since you now recognize the true happiness," she said, "and the things that falsely claim it for themselves, you now have to learn where you should go to get it, and whom you should ask for it."
"That indeed," I said, "I have long been eagerly wishing for. I have long been longing for that," said I. "But since even in the smallest matters," she said,
"as our Plato holds in the Timaeus, divine help ought to be implored, what do you think must be done now, so that we may be worthy to find the seat of that highest good?"

"But since Plato thinks, in his book the Timaeus, that one should beg for God's help even in small matters, what then do you think we must do so that we may find the chief seat of the foremost good?" "I think," I said, "that we must call upon the Father of all things, without whom no beginning is properly founded. I think," said I, "that we should call upon him without whom one can do nothing well." "Rightly!" she said, and at once she sang in measure thus. "You speak rightly," she said, and she sang thus in this metre:
PHILOSOPHY'S PRAYER TO GOD, THAT HE HIMSELF MAY SHOW THE HIGHEST GOOD. O Sower of the earth and heaven. You, Creator of heaven and earth,
You who govern the world by everlasting reason,

You order, shape and direct this world with your eternal wisdom. You who bid time go forth from eternity, that is, who commanded the times to begin at the beginning of the world. You bade the times begin their course together with the world, for before that there were no times, only eternity.
And, remaining unmoved yourself, you cause all things to move. And you yourself, steadfast, turn and change all things. For the heaven revolves and all things change.
You whom no outside causes drove
to fashion the work of flowing matter,

that is, matter formless and undistinguished. No other things drove you to make the shapeless material from which this world came. She means the undivided mass that he made first, in which nothing was yet distinguished. But, that is, nothing except, the form of the highest good planted within you, free from envy. Nothing but your own inward goodness, which has no envy. You, bearing the beautiful world in your mind,
you yourself most beautiful. You, who have always carried this beautiful world in your mind!

yourself more beautiful. You draw all things from the eternal pattern. You created it all according to the wisdom and the eternal image of your mind. And forming it in a like image, that is, you formed it. And you made it just as it was in your mind. No one made a model for you beforehand. And commanding ...
that is, you commanded the perfect parts to complete a perfect whole.

[Understand:] "work." And you commanded well-made parts to make a well-made work. For just as handsome limbs make a handsome man, so it also came about that every part of the world, being perfectly made, made the world perfectly made. If its parts were lacking, the world itself would be lacking. "You bind the elements by numbers," [understand:] "fixed ones." As if he were saying: you bind the four elements. You bind the four elements together in such a way "that cold things agree with flames,"

"dry things with liquid ones." That is, hot and cold, as fire and water are, and dry and wet, as earth and air are, do not fight each other. "So that the purer fire does not fly off." So firmly that the lighter fire, which has no murkiness in it, does not fly away upward because of its lightness, since it is uppermost.
"Or weights drag down the sunken earth." Nor does heaviness sink the earth downward.
"You, joining together the middle soul,"

"spread it out through harmonious members." That is, you join and spread out the soul through harmonious members. You fasten the soul to the limbs it loves, and divide it among them. I mean the sun, which moves in the middle of heaven and moves in the middle of the seven planets. The philosophers called it the soul of the world, because it passes through everything that grows green and grows, as the soul passes through the limbs. "Of threefold nature." It is of a threefold nature, because it shines, warms (as in brooding), and burns. Other fires burn too, but they do not warm in this way. "Moving all things," [understand:] to growth. It gives life to all things, as the soul gives life to our body.
"Which, when it has rolled its motion, divided into two circles." That is, which, when it leads around its course, divided into two hemispheres,

"goes to return into itself," that is, to its rising. And when it bends its journey, divided into two arcs, one above the earth and the other under the earth, it goes back again to its rising. "And it circles the deep mind and turns"
that is, it illuminates heaven "with a similar image."

And by night it travels the hidden path under the earth, and in the same way by day it travels across heaven above the earth. "You bring forth," that is, produce, "souls and lesser lives by like causes," that is, by a cause: that there should be beings who would obey God freely. For the same purpose you created angels and humans, who are lower than they. What was the cause? That they should acknowledge you as their creator and honor you. Or another reading: with like gifts you have raised angels and humans above the other animals, I mean reason and understanding.
"And fitting them, lofty, to light chariots." And raising them up high on swift senses.
"You sow them in heaven and on earth." You place them in heaven and on earth: angels in heaven, humans on earth. "Which," [understand:] souls and lives, "you, with kindly mind, cause, turned back,"
"to be turned to you, led back by fire."

You make them turn back to you, turned toward you, by your goodwill. "Grant, Father, to the mind," [understand:] his, "to ascend to the august seat." You who do this, grant his mind that it may climb up to your imperial throne, so that it may understand heavenly things.
"Grant it to survey," that is, to find, "the source of the good." Make his mind find the origin of the good. "The light having been found." And when he finds the light,
Grant that it may fix the clear sight of the mind on you. So let him hold fast on you the clear eyes of his mind.
Scatter the mists and the weights of the earthly mass. Drive away the blindness and the sins of the earthly body.
And shine with your splendor.

And shine upon them with your radiance. For you are clear calm. You are the clear brightness. You are the tranquil rest for the pious. You are the comfortable rest for those who will good. To see you is the end. When one sees you, that is the end.

You are also the beginning, the carrier, the leader, the path and the goal. You are the beginning. You are the one who carries us, that is, to the end. You are the guide, and you yourself are the way, and the end that we strive toward.

WHETHER THERE IS SOME HIGHEST GOOD. Since, then, you have seen what the form of the imperfect good is, and also that of the perfect. Since you have looked upon the image of both, of the imperfect good and of the perfect: namely, the form of the imperfect is the one that gives one of the five, and the form of the perfect is the one that gives all of them together. Now, I think, it must be shown
in what this perfection of happiness is established.

Therefore it must now be said where perfect happiness has its place, where its seat is. In this, I think, the first thing to ask is this. In this discussion I think we must first ask this: whether any good of this kind, such as you defined a little earlier, can exist in the nature of things. Whether any such good can exist among all things as you showed earlier, when you said: Unless I am mistaken, that is true and perfect happiness which makes a person self-sufficient, powerful, revered, renowned, and joyful. Let no empty image of our thought deceive us, apart from the truth of the thing that underlies it. Let no false image of our thought deceive us, without the truth of the substance, as the people of old thought about the manes and the demigods, and that thought deceived them.
But it cannot be denied that it exists, and that it is, as it were, a kind of fountain of all goods. No one can deny that it exists and that it is the source of all good. For everything
that is called imperfect, by a diminution of the perfect

is held to be imperfect. The imperfect is always called imperfect because it falls short of the full. Hence it follows that if in any kind something seems imperfect, there must also be something perfect in it. Hence it is necessary, if there is something lacking, that there is also something full of the same kind. That is an argument from the part to the whole. For if perfection is taken away,
one cannot even imagine where what is held to be imperfect would have come from.

On the other hand, if the full does not exist, no one need even think of the lacking. An argument from the whole to the part. For the nature of things did not take its beginning from diminished and unfinished things. For the nature of all things did not begin with lacking and unfinished things. Rather, setting out from whole and complete things, it slips down into these lowest and exhausted ones. Rather, beginning from whole and full things, it slid down afterwards until it came to these lowest and powerless things. Man has come from the delights of paradise to the miseries of this world. From immortality he has come to mortality. From the likeness of God he has become like the senseless beasts of burden.

"But if, as we showed a little earlier, there is a certain imperfect [?] of fragile good, it cannot be doubted that there is also a solid and perfect one." If there is an incomplete happiness, then there is no doubt that there is also a complete and whole one. "It has been concluded," I said, "most firmly and most truly." You have established it, I said, very firmly and very truly. What can be firmer or truer than when one supports the whole by the part, or the part by the whole?

WHERE THE HIGHEST GOOD IS. "Where it dwells," she said, "consider thus." Where it is, she said, work that out for yourself in this way. "That God, the ruler of all things, is good is proved by the common understanding of human minds." That God, the lord of all things, is good, every person's mind acknowledges. "For since nothing better than God can be conceived,

who would doubt that that than which nothing is better is good?" Since nothing better than God can be conceived, that than which nothing is better is necessarily good. The highest is necessarily high; the greatest is necessarily great; the best is necessarily good. This is an argument from the greater to the lesser. "Reason shows that God is good in such a way that it also proves that perfect good is in him." Thus this argument confirms that God is good, so that perfect good is in him. Since nothing is better than he, he is not merely good but perfectly good. "For if he were not such, he could not be the ruler of all things." If he is not perfectly good, then he is not the highest lord of things. "For there would be something more excellent than he, possessing perfect good,

which would seem to be prior to and older than him." For then there would be another, higher one, possessing perfect good, which would be prior to him and worthier than he. "For it has been made clear that all perfect things are prior to those less whole." For I said just now that all perfect things are prior to the deficient ones.

PREMISE. "Therefore, lest the reasoning proceed to infinity, it must be acknowledged that the highest God is most full of the highest and perfect good." Therefore it must be admitted, so that the argument does not become too long, that the foremost God is full of the foremost and perfect good.
PREMISE. "But we have established that perfect good is true happiness." Now it has been shown that perfect good is true happiness.
CONCLUSION.

"Therefore it is necessary that true happiness is situated in the highest God." Therefore true happiness is necessarily in God. The syllogism is made thus: In God is the highest good. The highest good and happiness are one and the same. Because that is so, happiness is there where the highest good is. "I accept it," I said. I understand it well, I said. "Nor is there anything that could in any way contradict it." Nor can anyone argue against it.

ON THE PREDICATIVE AND CONDITIONAL SYLLOGISM. Here two premises (sumpta) make one conclusion, because it is a predicative syllogism, just as in a conditional syllogism the proposition and the assumption also make the conclusion. What are sumpta but concessa, that is, in our language, "admissions"? When two things are admitted, the third necessarily follows from them, even without being admitted.

It is rightly called illatio (inference), because it is inferred (illatum) from two things taken, or, if it so happens, from three things taken. That means: thrown in along with them against one's will. But what is propositio (the major premise) except the first, far-reaching probing (temptatio), with which one first approaches the man and probes his admission from a distance? So also is assumptio (the minor premise): that which is taken up in addition to it, to probe his admission a second time. Because these two produce the third, by which the man is so caught that he cannot get away, it is therefore called conclusio, that is, 'lock.' The conditional syllogism (conditionalis syllogismus) takes its name from the fact that it speaks with conditions and with 'if': if this is, and this, then that is.

Therefore conditionalis means 'spoken with conditions.' But predicatiuus means 'spoken simply,' because it states plainly, without conditions and without 'if': this is so, and this; therefore that is so. The members of both are called in common predicationes, or proloquia, or propositiones, or enuntiationes. These four words we can all equally and in common interpret as 'statement.' Since an enuntiatio is, as Aristotle says in the Peri hermeneias (On Interpretation), a sentence that is true or false, and a predicatio is the same thing, and so are a propositio and a proloquium, what then are falsehoods and truths but statements?

But a syllogism must always have two statements of such a kind that they confirm the third. It cannot be otherwise: the first two must be so linked to each other that the second has half of the first, either the subject or the predicate (declarative part). And because the second repeats half of the first, whatever is left over unrepeated in either of them, when it is a predicative syllogism, makes the third. Whoever wishes to recognize this in other syllogisms, let him learn it here. One statement is: "The highest good is in God" (summum bonum est in deo). "The highest good" is the subject; "is in God" is the predicate. The other is: "The highest good is happiness" (summum bonum beatitudo est). There the subject part of the first is repeated.

The third is: "Happiness is in God" (beatitudo in deo est). That was what was left over in the first two, for from the one came "happiness," and from the other came "is in God." That is how it goes in a predicative syllogism. In a conditional one it goes much the same way. If we say: "If the sun is above the earth, it is day" (si sol super terram est, dies est), that is the proposition. The assumption takes half of it, thus: "But it is day" (dies autem est). What then still remains unrepeated in the proposition makes the conclusion, like this: "Therefore the sun is above the earth" (igitur sol est super terram). The subject is that part of a statement about which something is said; what is said about it is the predicate (declarative part).

Without this rule no syllogism comes about. As long as she taught him with arguments and examples, the discourse was easier. Because she now wishes to give him stronger remedies, she has therefore now begun to deal with him, in addition to the arguments, by means of syllogisms, which are the most powerful, both in dialectical disputation and in rhetorical persuasion.

THAT GOD IS IN HIS SUBSTANCE THE HIGHEST GOOD AND BLESSEDNESS, BECAUSE THERE IS NO DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THEM. "But I ask you," she said, "see how reverently and how firmly you prove what we said: that the highest God is completely full of the highest good." "Now I ask you," she said, "see how devoutly and how worthily you consider what I said: that the sovereign God is full of the most glorious good." "In what way?" I said. "What do you mean?" said I.

"Do not suppose that this Father of all things either received from outside that highest good of which he is said to be full, or has it by nature in such a way that you might think the substance of God, who has it, is different from the substance of the blessedness that he has."

"Do not think that the Lord of all things received the good of which he is full in this way. Do not think either that he has it from himself in such a way that the God who has it and the blessedness he has were not one substance. Neither of these two is true: he did not receive it, and it is not separate from his substance. For if you think it was received from outside, you could judge that the one who gave it is more excellent than the one who received it. If you think he received his highest good from somewhere else, you could consider the giver superior to the one who received it. But we most rightly confess that he is the most excellent of all things. And you know that we rightly declare him the highest of all things."

"But suppose it is in him by nature, yet different from him in concept. Since we are speaking of God, the ruler of all things, let whoever can imagine it say who joined these different things together."

"Now, he did not receive it. But if he has it from himself, and it is in any way unlike him, then let someone try to guess who joined them together, things so unlike: I mean God and his good. For we are speaking of God, the highest Lord of all things. Finally, whatever is different from any thing is not the thing from which it is understood to be different. To put it most exactly: whatever is unlike another is also other than the thing it is unlike. That is an argument from the dissimilar: things that are dissimilar cannot be one. Therefore, whatever is different by its nature from the highest good is not the highest good. Therefore it necessarily follows that that God is not the highest good
who is by nature in any way unlike the highest good. It is wicked to think this of him, than whom, as is established, nothing is more excellent.

"It is impious to think this of that God than whom nothing is superior. For no thing at all can have a nature better than its origin. No nature can be better than its origin. This is an argument from the efficient cause: the effect is necessarily such as its efficient cause is. That is why the proverb says: 'As the root, so also the branches.' How then can the highest good be better than God, who is its origin? He is its origin, but in such a way that he himself is it. Therefore, by the truest reasoning, I would conclude that what is the origin of all things is also, in its substance, the highest good. Therefore I can establish by true reasoning that God, who is the origin of all goods, is the highest good in his substance."

"Most rightly," I said. "Very rightly," I said, "have you established it," that is, because your arguments are true. "But it has been granted that the highest good is happiness." "So it was shown before," she said, "that the highest good is happiness." "So it is," I said.

"So it is," I said. "Therefore," she said, "it is necessary to acknowledge that God is happiness." "So it is also necessary," she said, "that God is not only the highest good but also happiness." That is the fitting conclusion. "I cannot," I said, "object to the premises set out before, and I see that this inference follows from them." "I cannot oppose the earlier statements," I said, "and I see that this later one follows from them of necessity."
LIKEWISE A SUBTLER ARGUMENT: THAT THINGS WHICH ARE DIFFERENT ARE NOT HIGHEST GOODS, AND THAT THINGS WHICH ARE HIGHEST ARE NOT DIFFERENT.
"Consider," she said, "whether the same thing may be proved more firmly from this as well:
that two goods which are different from each other cannot be highest." "Now consider for yourself whether it will also be proved by these arguments that two unlike goods cannot be the highest."
PREMISE. "For it is clear that goods which differ are not such that the one is what the other is." "I have shown before that dissimilar goods cannot be one."
PREMISE. "Therefore neither of them can be perfect, since the one is lacking to the other." "Therefore neither is a full good, since neither is together with the other."
INFERENCE. But that what is not perfect

is not the highest is manifest. What is not complete cannot be the foremost. The syllogism is constructed thus: Unlike goods are not one. Things that are not one are both deficient. What is deficient never becomes the foremost. Which are the unlike goods? Riches and glory. How are they deficient? In that each of them lacks the share [?] of the others. Because that is so, that which lacks anything cannot be the foremost.
LIKEWISE A PREMISE. "In no way, therefore, can those goods that are highest be different." "Those, on the other hand, which are the highest are not unlike."
PREMISE. "But we have concluded that both happiness and God are the highest good." "Now I have shown before that God and happiness are the highest."

CONCLUSION. "Therefore it is necessary that whatever is the highest divinity is itself the highest happiness." "Therefore it is necessary that the divinity, which is the highest of all things, is the highest happiness." This syllogism too is constructed thus: The highest goods are not unlike. God and happiness are the highest. Because each of them is what the other also is (I mean, because each of them is the highest good), therefore they are one. "Nothing," I said, "can be concluded that is truer in fact, firmer in reasoning, or more worthy of God." "Now," I said, "nothing can be established that is truer, nor more reasonable, nor more befitting God."
PRESENTATION OF A GIFT FOR ARGUMENTS WELL UNDERSTOOD. "In addition to these things," she said, "just as geometers are accustomed, once propositions have been demonstrated, to infer something further,
which they themselves call porisms, so I too will give you something like a corollary."

When I had answered her in this way, she said: "Geometers have the custom," she said, "after propositions have been demonstrated, of giving their pupils something extra that was not asked for. They call that addition a 'questum' [gain]. So I give you, as a gain, what I now tell you without being asked, just as if I were giving you a corollary. For since people become blessed by attaining blessedness, and blessedness is itself divinity, it is clear that they become blessed by attaining divinity." Because people become blessed by gaining blessedness, and God is blessedness, whoever gains God is blessed. An argument from the efficient cause. Because God and blessedness are one, they make people blessed. An argument of this kind holds a twofold cause of its effect, in the manner of a syllogism, because it says: if this and this is so.
then that is so. "But just as men become just by attaining justice, and wise by attaining wisdom, so those who have attained divinity must become gods

by the same reasoning." And further: just as people become just by gaining justice, and wise by gaining wisdom, so in the same way they must also become gods by gaining God. An argument from the similar: as that attainment acts, so this one acts as well. That is similitude. "Therefore every blessed man is a god." Because that is so, the blessed man is a god. Because God and blessedness are one, they also make people one with him. This is still an argument from the efficient, that is, from the cause. "But by nature there is indeed only one; by participation, however, nothing prevents there being very many." But take good note of this distinction: only one God exists by nature; many can become gods through grace

by having a share in him. With this she has given him a gift. "And this is beautiful and precious," I said, "whether you prefer to call it a porisma or a corollary." "Now it is also very beautiful," I said, "whether you call it a porisma or a corollary." The common honors of victory for all victors were palms in their hands and laurel crowns on their heads. But to those who did something very glorious in war, or also in games and public shows, a precious head ornament was given. Because it looked like a corolla, that is, a crown, it was called a corollarium. Suetonius therefore speaks about the generosity of Caesar Augustus

in these words: "And so, even at shows and games given by others, he frequently offered large corollaries and prizes from his own resources. He attended no Greek contest at which he did not honor each of the contestants according to his merit."

WHETHER THE THINGS THAT BELONG TO BLESSEDNESS SHOULD BE CALLED ITS PARTS, OR WHETHER THEY ARE ALL REFERRED TO ONE OF THEM. "And yet nothing is more beautiful than this, which reason persuades us to add to these points." "Nothing," she said, "is more beautiful than what reason teaches us to add here." "What is it?" I said. "What is that?" said I.

"Since blessedness seems to contain many things," she said, "do all these things join together as one body of blessedness, as it were, through a certain variety of parts? Or is there some one of them that makes up the substance of blessedness,

and to which the rest are referred?" Since blessedness includes many things, such as the good and the five things mentioned above, are these parts of blessedness, just as the body has various limbs? Or is one of them blessedness, with the others looking toward it? She has already stated very precisely that the highest good is blessedness. Now she wants to say that the other five aim at that highest good. "I would like you to make this clear," I said, "by naming the things themselves." "I would like you to explain this to me," I said, "by speaking about the thing itself."
THAT BLESSEDNESS HAS NO PARTS. "Do we not consider blessedness to be the good?" she said. "Should we not consider blessedness good?" she said. "Indeed, the highest good," I said.

"Yes, even the foremost," I said. "You may add this to all of them," she said. "You must apply 'highest' to all five," she said. "For the same thing, namely blessedness, is judged to be the highest sufficiency, and the same is the highest power, and also reverence, renown, and pleasure: these are judged to be blessedness." Just as blessedness is the highest good, so it is also the highest sufficiency and the highest power. It is also the highest reverence and renown.
and pleasure. "What then? Are all these, the good, sufficiency, power and the rest, as it were members of happiness?

What do you think? Are all these, I mean the good and sufficiency and power and the others, like limbs of happiness? Or are they all referred to the good as to a summit? Or do they all aim at the good, as if it were their head?" "I understand," I said, "what you put forward to be investigated, but I want to hear what you decide." "I understand well," I said, "what you are giving me to puzzle out; but I long to hear how you explain it." "Take the distinction of this matter as follows." "Now listen," she said, "I will teach you to distinguish it! I will teach you how they aim at the good

and do not make up the good itself as parts. If all these were members of happiness, they would also differ from one another." This is how you should proceed toward it by argument: if the good and the other five were limbs of happiness, they would be unlike one another. That is an argument from adjuncts: dissimilarity is always joined to members. "For this is the nature of parts, that being diverse they make up one body."

Such is always the nature of parts, that being unlike one another they make up one body. "But all these have been shown to be the same." Now these have been shown to be one being. "Therefore they are by no means members." Therefore they are not members. Because they are one, they are not diverse. That is an argument from contraries, for being one and being diverse are contradictory. Because they are not diverse, they are not members either. That is, as I just said, from adjuncts. "Otherwise happiness would seem to be put together from one member, which cannot happen." Otherwise happiness would have to be made out of one limb, which cannot be. No composition can come from just one thing. That again is an argument from contraries, for being simple and being composite are contradictory.
"That indeed," I said, "is not in doubt." "There is no doubt about that," I said. "But I am waiting for what remains." "Next I am waiting for what is still to come."

THAT THE THINGS WHICH BELONG TO HAPPINESS ARE REFERRED TO ONE. But it is plain that all the other things are referred to the good. The other five, which together are one with the good, are directed toward the good, because people want to reach the good by means of them. For sufficiency is sought because it is judged to be good. That is why people desire sufficiency: because it is considered good. Power is sought because it too is believed to be good. That is also why power is prized: because it seems good to people.
The same may be inferred about reverence, renown and pleasure. I can say the same about the other three.
"Therefore the good is the sum and the cause of all things that are sought." Therefore the good is always

the head and purpose of all that one desires. For what keeps in itself no good, either in reality or by resemblance, cannot be sought in any way. But what is not good, nor like the good, no one desires. And conversely, things that are not good by nature are still sought as if they were truly good, if they seem to be good. And on the other hand, things that are not really good, if only they resemble it, are desired for that very reason, as if they were good. Hence it comes about
that goodness is rightly believed to be the highest hinge and cause of all things that are sought.

Therefore one must believe that goodness is always the innermost hinge and the truest spur of all desiring. But the thing for whose sake something is sought seems to be what is most wanted. Whatever anything is desired for, that is what one is chiefly striving after in it. For example, if someone wished to ride for the sake of his health, he does not so much want the motion of riding as the effect of health. So the man who rides for his health is not after the stirring-up he gets from riding, but after becoming healthier. Since, then, all things are sought for the sake of the good, it is not they but the good itself that is desired by everyone. From this it is clear that whatever anyone desires for the sake of the good, he does not desire that thing, but the good.
AGAIN. But we have agreed that happiness is the thing for whose sake the other things are desired. But the good, for whose sake each thing was desired,

I said was happiness. Therefore in this way too, happiness alone is sought. Therefore in this way as well, by seeking only the good (I mean), it is happiness alone that is sought. From this it is clearly evident that the good itself and happiness have one and the same substance. From this it is plainly seen that the good and blessedness are one thing.
I see no reason why anyone could disagree. "I know of nothing there that anyone could argue against," I said.
AGAIN. But we have shown that God and true happiness are one and the same. "Now I have shown," she said, "that God and blessedness are one."

"That is so," I said. "That is so," I said. Therefore we may safely conclude that his substance too lies in the good itself and nowhere else. "Therefore," she said, "I may boldly affirm that God's own substance lies in the good."
AN INVITATION TO HAPPINESS. Come here together, all you captives. Come here together, all who are in distress.
whom deceitful desire, dwelling in (that is, possessing) earthly minds, binds with wicked chains. You whom evil lusts, which possess your minds, bind with strong chains.
This will be your rest from your labours.
Here you will find rest: a house of refuge.

open to the wretched. This alone is the asylum of the guilty, which always stands open to the wretched. This is more certain than the one the descendants of Hercules made at Athens, who feared for their lives because of his guilt; or the one Romulus made at Rome as a refuge for fugitives.
Whatever the Tagus gives with its golden sands,
or the Hermus with its glowing red bank,
or the Indus, which lies near the hot part of the world,
mixing green stones with white ones,

does not light up the sight. Whatever the Tagus, a river of Spain, gives in its golden gravel, and the Hermus, a river of Asia Minor, on its gold-coloured bank, or the Indus, which is nearest of all to the eastern sun, mixing green gems, such as the emerald, with white ones, such as pearls, none of these opens the eyes of a man's mind.
Rather, they hide blind minds in their own, that is, their accustomed, darkness. Instead, they push blind minds further into their familiar darkness.
Whatever pleases here and stirs minds,
the earth has nourished in its inmost caverns. Whatever of this pleases a man or stirs his mind, the earth breeds in its bosom.
The splendour by which heaven is ruled and has its strength
shuns the dark shadows of the mind. But the radiance of God's wisdom, which rules heaven and makes it firm, shuns the dim darkness of the mind.
Whoever is able to perceive this light
will deny that the rays of Phoebus are bright. Whoever is able to see that light will not say that the sun has bright radiance.

THAT THE ONE AND THE GOOD ARE THE SAME. I agree, I said. I affirm it, I said. For everything holds together, linked by the firmest reasons. All your arguments are certain and strengthened by firm reasoning. They are made fast with arguments and syllogisms. Then she said:
How highly will you value it if you come to know what the good itself is?

Yes, she then said, how precious does it seem to you if you consider what the good itself is? Infinitely, I said. Beyond measure precious, I said. For it also lets me recognize God, who is the good. If by it I may also come to know God,
who is good. Yet, she said, I will make this plain by the truest reasoning. Truly, she said, I will reveal it to you with very true argument. Only let what was concluded a little earlier stand.

Only keep in your memory the things that were established before. They will stand. They do, I said. Did we not show, she said, that the things most people seek are not true and perfect goods, because they differ from one another? Have I not shown you by argument, she said, that the goods many people desire are therefore neither true nor perfect, because they are separated? And that since each one lacked what another had, it could not bring full and absolute good? And that since each lacks another, it cannot by itself give full good, nor complete good?
But that they become the true good when they are gathered as it were into one form and one effective power, so that what is sufficiency is also power.

reverence, renown, and pleasure? And how would they then become the good, if they joined together as if into one form and one working, so that what one of the five is, the others are as well? If there were five highest goods, there would also be five beatitudes, and there would also be five of the workings, because each one by itself would make a person blessed. Unless all are one and the same, they have nothing by which they could be counted among the things to be sought. And have I not shown you this: unless they are one, they have nothing of what is to be desired, because one without the others can do nothing?
It has been shown, I said. "It has been shown," I said. Nor can it be doubted in any way. There is no doubt about it at all.
PREMISE. Therefore those things which, when they are at variance, are not good at all, but which become good once they have begun to be one, is it not

by attaining unity that they come to be good? Those things, she said, that are not good while they are at variance, but become good when they are united: did they not become good because the One came to them? So it seems, I said. That seems so to me, I said.

PREMISE. But do you grant that everything that is good is good by participating in the good, or not? And everything that is good, she said, as the five are once they are no longer separate: do you grant that it is good by participating in the good, which is the One, or do you not grant it? It is so. That is so: it is good, I said.

CONCLUSION. By similar reasoning, then, you must grant that one and good are the same. By the same reasoning, she said, you must necessarily grant that one and good are not separate. If you grant two things, you must necessarily grant the third. The syllogism is made like this: what is not good becomes good from the One. So then it has become good from the good! I mean from the One. Therefore one and good are not separate. For things whose effect is not by nature different have the same substance. Things whose action is not separate must have a substance that is not separate. Goodness makes a thing good by its participation in itself, and so does the One. Therefore they have one action. I cannot deny it, I said. I can never deny that, I said.
