clearly become happy! But it is fitting that those who are happy are gods. And recognize by argument that, since the good is happiness, all the good, because they are good, are also happy.

and those who are blessed are, by that, gods. What reward can be equal to that? The syllogism stands above. Therefore the reward of the good is one that no day wears away, no one's power diminishes, and no one's wickedness darkens: to become gods. So the reward of the good is one that no one spoils, no one's power diminishes, and no one's wickedness hinders: that they become gods.

WHAT THE STADIUM AND THE OLYMPIAD ARE. Among the Greeks a festival was established long ago, which they called the Olympiad, after Mount Olympus in Macedonia, near which it was first held. Later they held it by the Alpheus, a river of Arcadia, where it runs between the cities of Elis and Pisa,

because there are beautiful fields there. The festival was established so that there would be a public testing of all skills. That is why the testing was called pancratios in Greek. There was no one in all Greece who measured himself in any glorious thing by which he wanted to win glory who did not show it there, at the Olympiad. If he was confident in wrestling, he was called palestricator in Greek. If he was confident in fighting with the club, he was called pugil. If he fought with the sword, he was called gladiator. If he fought with the cestus, which we call 'with bundles' [?], he was called agonitheta, that is, contestant. If he wanted to compete in a contest on his chariot, that was called curule certamen. If he wanted to show how well he could move up in the air,

he did that by walking over the rope, which was called funiambulum. If he also wanted to show his speed, he did that by running in the stadium, as those did at the tomb of Anchises of whom Virgil tells. Stadium was the name of the actual distance that they had to run. It is named in Greek from exercise. This distance was 125 paces, that is, the ninth part of a mile. For all of them their reward was ready there, provided publicly. The reward was called brabion in Greek and bravium in Latin.

ON THE CERTAIN PUNISHMENT OF THE WICKED. Since these things are so, no wise man can doubt that the wicked also suffer a punishment that cannot be separated from them. So let no wise man doubt that the evil, too, are never without punishment. For since good and evil,
and likewise punishment and reward, stand face to face in opposition, whatever we see happen in the reward of the good must have its counterpart, on the opposite side, in the punishment of the evil.

Since good and evil, reward and punishment, are opposed to each other, it must be that what happens in the reward of the good and in the punishment of the evil is also opposed. What is that? Therefore, just as for the upright their uprightness itself becomes their reward, so for the wicked their wickedness itself is their punishment. That is what you can learn here: just as the reward of the good is their goodness, so the torment of the evil is their evil itself.
Now whoever is afflicted with punishment does not doubt that he is afflicted with an evil. I think that whoever suffers any punishment

acknowledges that what he suffers is evil. If, then, they are willing to judge themselves, can they consider themselves free of punishment, when wickedness, the worst of all evils, not only affects them, that is, afflicts them, but also deeply infects them, that is, corrupts them? Therefore, how can they suppose themselves to be without punishment, if they are willing to think about themselves, that is, if they are willing to perceive anything about themselves at all, when wickedness, the greatest of all evil, not only torments them but even corrupts them? This is an argument from effect: because they are infected, it is clear from that how severely they are afflicted.
But look, from the opposite side, that of the good, at what punishment accompanies the wicked. Consider also, from the side of the good, what punishment falls on the evil. For everything that is,
you learned a little earlier that it is one, and that the one itself is good. From this it follows

that everything that exists also appears to be good. I taught you this syllogism before: that everything that exists is one, and that the one is good. Those are two premises, and the conclusion necessarily follows from them: that everything that exists is good. In this way, therefore, whatever falls away from the good ceases to be. Attached to this conclusion, in turn, is this one: whatever is not good does not exist. When one conclusion follows from another, as Martianus says, that is called confinis conclusio ('adjoining conclusion') in Latin and simplerasma in Greek.

HOW THOSE GIVEN OVER TO VARIOUS VICES ARE TO BE REGARDED. So it comes about that the wicked cease to be what they had been, that is, men. From this it follows that the wicked are not the men they were when they were not wicked. But the remaining shape of the human body still shows that they were men. But that they were men is shown by the human form itself, which they still have. Therefore, having turned to wickedness, they have also lost their human nature. Because they turned to evil,
they lost their human nature. But since goodness alone can raise anyone above men, it must be that those whom wickedness has cast down from the human condition

it thrusts down below what a man deserves. But since goodness alone can raise anyone above men, so that he becomes a god, it must be that those whom their wickedness throws down from manhood are at once made lower than men. It follows, then, that you cannot consider a man someone you see transformed by vices. Hence you cannot take for a man someone you see changed by vices.
Does he burn with greed, a violent robber of other people's wealth [apum, probably for opum]? You would call him like a wolf. If he grows greedy and robs other people of their property by force,
then he is like a wolf. Is he fierce and restless, exercising his tongue in quarrels? You will compare him to a dog. One who is fierce with his tongue and never stops quarrelling is like a dog.
Is he a secret plotter who delights in having stolen by fraud? Let him be ranked with little foxes. So it is with one who secretly sets out to gain something

with treachery, people call him a fox. If he cannot control his anger and rages, let him be believed to carry the mind of a lion. That is, whoever has no restraint in his anger and is always raging carries the spirit of a lion.
If he is timid and quick to run, and dreads things that are not to be feared, let him be considered like the deer. Whoever is needlessly fearful and given to flight should seem to you like a stag.
Is he sluggish and dull, sunk in torpor? He lives the life of an ass. One who is idle and slack, and shrinks from work, lives like an ass.
Is he fickle and inconstant, changing his pursuits? He is no different from birds. One who is light-minded and unsteady in what he takes up is like a bird.
Is he sunk in foul and unclean lusts?

He is held fast by the pleasure of a filthy sow. One who gives himself over to shameful and unclean lusts is like a sow that has wallowed in the mire. So it comes about that one who abandons goodness and ceases to be a man, since he cannot pass into the divine condition, is turned into a beast. So it happens that one who has given up goodness is not a man, and since he cannot attain to the dignity of God, he becomes a beast.
THAT IT IS NOT SO HARMFUL FOR THE BODY TO BE TURNED INTO A BEAST AS TO BE CLOTHED WITH A BEAST'S MIND. The sails of the Neritian leader, that is, Ulysses, whose homeland was the island of Neritus,
and his ships wandering on the sea
the east wind drove to the island
where the beautiful goddess dwelling there,
born of the seed of the Sun,
mixes for her new guests, that is, those who have just arrived,

cups touched with a spell. I can remind you of a great horror, which is still not equal to this horror. What is it? When Ulysses was returning from Troy, he wandered far over the sea, and he traveled from Sicily toward Italy. Then the wind drove him out with his ships to the island that is called Aeaea. There the beautiful Circe, daughter of the Sun, who dwelt there, poured bewitched drink for these same guests.
When the hand powerful in herbs turned them into various shapes,
the face of a boar covers this one;
that one, a Marmaric lion, that is, from the province of Africa, Marmarica,
grows teeth and claws;
this one, newly added to the wolves,
howls when he means to weep;
that one, like an Indian tiger, walks tamely around the house.

So when the magic hand changed them into various forms, one was like a boar, one like the lion; and one who had also become a wolf stood and howled when he wanted to weep. And one also went around the house, made like a tiger.
But although the divinity of the winged Arcadian,
pitying the leader beset by various ills,
freed him from the plague of his hostess,
yet the oarsmen had already drunk the evil cups.

And yet Mercury, flying like a bird, who was raised on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia, out of pity freed the distressed leader from the poison of his hostess; yet the companions had already drunk the evil drink. Mercury is painted 'alatis talariis', that is, with feathered shoes, which the Greeks call 'petasi'. He warned Ulysses to avoid Circe. But when it happened that he came there against his will, and she poured drink for the others, which he would not drink, then Mercury gave him a remedy for it
with his staff,
which was called the caduceus, and which was healing against all things. 'Already the swine had exchanged the food of Ceres for acorns.' And having become swine, they exchanged bread for acorns.
And nothing remains whole,
voice and body being lost. And they were completely lost, in limbs and in voice.
Only the mind, unchanged, groans
over the monstrous things it suffers.
Only the mind stood firm, grieving over the horror that had happened to it. O hand far too weak,
nor the power of herbs,
which, though they can change the limbs,
cannot change the hearts. Indeed, how weighty that was! What could the herbs and the poisoning hand achieve, which harmed the limbs but could not harm the mind?
Within lies the strength of men,
hidden away in a secret citadel. The power lies within. There the strengths of man are deeply hidden.
These poisons, that is, vices,
drag a man away from himself more powerfully. The poisons I speak of make a man less master of himself.
Which pass dreadfully deep within,
and do not harm the body,
but rage with a wound to the mind. These strike deeper in. They do not harm the limbs, but attack the mind.

THAT THE WICKED WOULD BE LESS WRETCHED IF THEY WERE NOT PERMITTED TO SIN. Then I said: "I admit it, and I see that it is not wrong to say that the vicious, though they keep the outward form of the body, are still changed into beasts by the nature of their minds." "I grant you that," I said then, "and I know that I rightly call the wicked beasts, since they have beastly minds, although in their bodies they are like men."
"But those whose savage and wicked mind rages for the destruction of the good: I would not have wished that very thing to be permitted to them."

"But that those whose minds are so damned and so evil may persecute the good: that is what I would not want." "Nor is it permitted," she said. "No," she said, "they may not. As will be shown in a fitting place. As you will learn well when I bring you to it. But yet if that very thing which is believed to be permitted to them were taken away, the punishment of wicked men would be relieved in great part. But if that very thing which you think they are allowed were taken from them, their punishment would be lightened by it."

PROPOSITION. For, though it may perhaps seem unbelievable to someone, the wicked are necessarily more unhappy when they have accomplished what they desired than if they could not fulfill what they desire.
Truly, though many do not believe it can happen, the wicked are the more unhappy for doing their will than if they could not do it.

ASSUMPTION. For if it is wretched to have willed wicked things, it is more wretched to have been able to do them. If willing evil is wretched, being able to do evil is more wretched still. Without this ability, the effect of a wretched will would languish. For an evil will could not show itself without it.
CONCLUSION. Therefore, since each has its own misery,
those whom you see willing a crime must be oppressed by a threefold misfortune:

to be able, to accomplish. Therefore they are necessarily unhappy in three ways, since there are three miseries: I mean willing, being able, and doing what is evil. That is a rhetorical syllogism, because it is more diffuse. A dialectical one is more contracted, because it scarcely has [anything beyond] the subject part and the declarative part in each proposition. 'I grant it,' I said. 'I grant you that,' said I.

THAT THE WICKED WOULD BE MOST UNHAPPY EVEN IF THEY NEVER DIED. "But I earnestly wish that they may soon be free of this misfortune, deprived of the power to commit crime. May God grant that they lose the power to do evil and so be rid of that unhappiness very soon."
"They will be free of it," she said, "sooner than you perhaps wish, or than they think they will be free of it.

So they will," she said. "They will be rid of it even faster than you might perhaps wish, or than they suppose. For within such short bounds of life (that is, spans of life) nothing comes so late that an immortal mind (that is, a wise one) should think it a long wait. Nor in the term of this short life is there anything so slow in coming that any eternal mind would think it too long to wait for. The wise man, who knows eternity, counts temporal things as nothing. Their great hope
and lofty structure of crimes is often destroyed by a sudden and unexpected end.

Their powerful hope and their great preparation for evil are often felled by death, suddenly and unexpectedly. Which indeed sets a limit to their misery. That at least limits their wretchedness. For if wickedness makes men wretched, then the longer a man is wicked, the more wretched he must be. For if evil makes men wretched, then the longer a man is evil, the more wretched he must necessarily be. That is an argument from the lesser to the greater. Since even wickedness that is only beginning makes men wretched, much more, she says, does wickedness that keeps growing.
I would judge them the most unhappy of all, if at least death in the end did not finish their malice.

I would say that they were the most wretched of all, if death did not at least put an end to their evil. That again is an argument from the lesser. For a man who has long been wicked is unhappier than one who is only beginning; therefore one who is always wicked would be the most unhappy. For this reason she says next: For if we have reached a true conclusion about the misfortune of depravity, it is clear that a misery which is known to be eternal is infinite. If what I said earlier is true, namely, 'if wickedness makes men wretched, the man who is wicked longer must be more wretched,' then it is certain that the misery which is eternal is infinite, and therefore the most unhappy. If long-lasting depravity is more wretched than brief depravity, then everlasting depravity is necessarily both infinite and most unhappy.

She strengthens this argument so carefully because she is concerned that he might distrust it. Who can easily believe that the wicked, if they lived forever and forever went unpunished, could be the most unhappy and most wretched of all from their injustice alone? So hear his answer. Then I said: Then I answered her. A wondrous inference indeed, I said, and hard to concede. That is a wondrous conclusion, I said, and hard to believe. But I recognize that it agrees all too well with what was conceded before.

But I see well that it agrees with the earlier admissions. You judge rightly, she said. You think rightly, she said. But whoever thinks it hard to accept the conclusion should, in fairness, either demonstrate that something false came before it, or show that the arrangement of the propositions does not produce a necessary conclusion. But whoever is reluctant to believe this conclusion should show that what came before, by which I supported it, is false, or else he should argue that those same statements, even if they are true, are not arranged in such a way as to produce this conclusion. Otherwise, once the premises are conceded, there is nothing at all to object to in the inference. Otherwise, if he simply grants the premises, he cannot deny the conclusion. She says this because the premise is often false.

as this one does: "No wise man despises riches." And so it does not support the conclusion that follows, which is: "Therefore Socrates, because he despised riches, was not wise." Often the first two premises are true, as these are: "Every wise man despises riches" and "Yet many wise men are rich." But they are not arranged so that they support this third statement: "Socrates, if he were wise, would be rich." Every way that syllogisms and arguments can go wrong comes down to these two faults. That is why arguments in which they are found are called sophistical. Anyone who wants fuller examples of these deceptive syllogisms should take them from Cicero's Rhetorics.
THAT THE WICKED WHO ARE HANDED OVER TO JUST PUNISHMENTS AT DEATH ARE HAPPIER THAN IF THEY REMAINED UNPUNISHED.
"For what I am about to say also seems no less astonishing, but it follows just as necessarily from what has been assumed, that is, from what has been granted."

"What I am going to tell you next," she said, "will seem just as great a wonder to you, and yet it necessarily follows from what was admitted earlier." "What is that?" I said. "What is it?" I said. "The wicked," she said, "are happier when they pay their punishments than if no penalty of justice restrained them. The wicked who suffer just punishment are happier than they would be if they did not suffer it. And I am not now attempting to argue what might occur to anyone,
that depraved morals are corrected by retribution and brought back to what is right by fear of punishment.

I am not saying that evil habits are punished and corrected by penalty, as someone might suppose. He need not suppose it, for that is not what I mean. "Nor that it serves as an example to others to avoid blameworthy things," that is, an example to others, so that they avoid guilt and do not do the same. "But I hold that the wicked are happier when punished in some other way, even if no account is taken of correction and no regard is given to example." Rather, I consider it in another way: that the wicked are the happier for paying for their sins, even though it is neither a correction for them nor an example to others.
"And what other way will there be," I said, "besides these?"
"What other way can there be," I said, "besides these?" And she said: "Have we not granted that the good are happy

but the wicked are wretched?" "Did we not agree," she said, "that the good are happy and the wicked wretched?" "So it is," I said. "That is so," I said. "If then," she said, "some good is added to someone's wretchedness,
Is he not happier than the one whose misery is pure and solitary,

without the admixture of any good? If then good is added to the misery of one of them, is that one not happier than the one with whose misery no good is mixed? 'So it seems,' I said. 'That seems likely,' said I. 'What if another evil were added to that same wretched man who lacks all goods, besides those by which he is wretched? Must he not be judged much unhappier than the one whose misfortune is relieved by a share in some good?' If also some other misery were added to the wretched man who lacks all good, besides the one from which he is wretched, would he not then be unhappier than that one whose misery is lightened by the mixture of some good? That is an argument from the contrary. For if anyone is made happy by good being added, he is necessarily also made unhappy by evil being added. 'Why not?' I said. 'How else?' said I.
"So when the wicked are punished, they do have something good attached to them, namely the punishment itself,

which is good by reason of justice." So she said: when the wicked are being punished, they have some good mixed in with them. I mean the punishment itself, which is good because it is just. "And when the same people escape punishment, there is something more of evil in them: the impunity itself, which you have admitted is evil because of its injustice." And while they are without punishment, they have in them, besides their wickedness, another evil: the impunity itself, which is evil because it is unjust.
"I cannot deny it." "I cannot deny that," I said. "So the wicked are much more unhappy when they are granted unjust impunity

than when punished with just vengeance. Therefore, she said, the wicked are unhappier when let go in unjust impunity than when justly punished. 'But it is plain that it is just for the wicked to be punished, and unjust for them to escape unpunished.' Therefore it is plainly right that the wicked pay for their wickedness, and plainly wrong that they go unpunished for it. 'Who would deny that?' 'Who can deny that?' said I.

"But no one will deny this either," she said, "that everything that is just is good, and conversely that what is unjust is evil." "Nor will anyone deny this either," she said, "but that what is right is good, and what is wrong is evil." Then I answered: "These things indeed follow from those that were concluded a little before." Then I answered her this: "These things," I said, "follow necessarily from those that were established in the earlier chapter." This chapter affirms that one: since they would be most unhappy, as she said before, if they were forever to remain unpunished, so they necessarily become happier when they are punished.

QUESTION. "But I ask you," I said, "do you allow (that is, grant) no punishments of souls after the body has been ended by death?" "Now, God protect [us] [?]," I said, "is there any punishment of souls after death?"

ANSWER. "Yes, and great ones," she said. "Yes, and mighty ones," she said. "Some of them, I think, are carried out with penal harshness, and others with purifying mercy." Some of them, I know, befall souls as vengeance, leading to damnation, and some as mercy, leading to purification. "But I do not intend to discuss these now." "But I have no wish to speak about them now."

A RECAPITULATION OF WHAT HAS BEEN SAID FROM THE BEGINNING OF THIS BOOK UP TO HERE. Up to now we have argued this, so that you would recognize that the power of the wicked, which seemed to you most unworthy, is nothing. I pursued this up to here, she said, so that you would recognize that the power of the wicked, which grieved you so much, is nothing. And those whom you complained of as unpunished,
you would see are never without punishments

for their wickedness. And you saw that those whom you said went unpunished for their wickedness are in no way without punishment. The licence which you prayed might quickly be ended, you learned is not long. And you learned that the freedom you prayed might quickly come to an end [?] is short. And that it would be more unhappy if it lasted longer, and most unhappy if it were eternal. And you came to know that it would be the more unhappy if it were long-lasting, and the most unhappy of all if it were eternal. After this, that the wicked are more wretched when let off with unjust impunity than when punished with just vengeance. And that those left unpunished for their wickedness are more wretched than those who are punished.

From this conclusion it follows that they are pressed by heavier punishments precisely when they are believed to go unpunished. From this it necessarily follows that they suffer the sharpest punishments when people think them unpunished for what they do. Then I said: Then I answered her.
When I consider your reasoning, I said, I think nothing truer could be said. But if I turn back to the judgments of men, who is there to whom these things would seem not only worth believing,
but even worth hearing? When I examine what you say, I said, I would know of nothing truer. But if I think of people's opinion, who is there who would believe it, or even be willing to hear it?

THE LIGHT OF REASON DOES NOT SHINE FOR DARKENED MINDS. It is so, she said. It is so, she said. For they cannot lift eyes accustomed to darkness to the light of clear truth. They cannot lift their eyes, accustomed to the darkness, up to the light. And they are like birds whose sight the night lights up and the day blinds. And they are like the birds that the day blinds and the night makes able to see, such as eagle-owls, screech-owls, and the night-raven. For since they look not at the order of things but at their own desires, they think that licence
or impunity for crimes is happy.

Since they look at their own will, not at the order that reason gives to things, they think that freedom to sin and going unpunished are happy. But see what the eternal, that is, the divine, law ordains. But you, see how God's law means it. If you have shaped your mind to better things, there is no need of a judge to bestow a reward:
you have yourself joined yourself to the more excellent. If you have turned your efforts toward worse things,
do not look for an avenger outside yourself: you yourself have thrust yourself down into the worse.

By turning toward the better, you have raised yourself up; there need be no assessor who thanks you for it. But if you turn yourself toward evil, then do not think about who else will avenge it; you yourself have harmed yourself. "Just as if you were to look in turn at the filthy earth and at the sky, with all things outside ceasing, by the very act of seeing you would seem to be now in the mud, now among the stars." Just as if you looked alternately up to heaven and down to the earth, and, without the doing of anyone else, from your own looking you are one moment in heaven and another moment in the mud. "But the common people do not regard these things." But the people do not know that. "What then?" What then shall we do?
Shall we side with these, whom we have shown to be like beasts?

Shall we, because of that, attach ourselves to those whom we said were like animals? What if someone, having entirely lost his sight, should even forget that he had ever had the power of seeing, and should think that nothing was lacking to him for human perfection?

Would we, seeing the same things, i.e. the loss of his eyes, think we were blind? What if he whose eyes have been taken away forgot that he once had them, and maintained that he was whole in every way? Should we then, who saw him eyeless, be counted blind?
HE WHO INFLICTS INJURY IS MORE WRETCHED THAN HE WHO SUFFERS IT. For they will not even agree to this, which rests equally on strong foundations
of reasons: that those who do injury are more unhappy than those who suffer it.

Nor do they admit this, which is just as certain from firm reasoning: that he who does wrong to another is more wretched than he who suffers it. "I would like," I said, "to hear these very reasons." "I would like," said I, "to hear the argument from which I might know that." "Do you deny," she said, "that every wicked person deserves punishment?" "Will you deny," said she, "that the wicked man is worthy of torment?" "Not at all." "No," said I. "It is clear in many ways that those who are wicked are unhappy." "Now it is plain in many ways," said she, "that those are unhappy

who are evil. "So it is," I said. "So it is," I said. "Those, then, who deserve punishment you do not doubt are wretched." "Those who deserve torment," she said, "you know to be wretched." "Agreed," I said.

"That is fitting," I said. "If, then," she said, "you sat as judge, on whom would you think punishment should be inflicted: on the one who had done the injury, or on the one who had suffered it?" "If you were a judge sitting in court," she said, "which would you think deserved the punishment: the one who did the wrong, or the one who endured it?"
"Nor do I doubt," I said, "that I would give satisfaction to the one who suffered by the pain of the one who did it."

"I would not doubt," said I, "but that I should satisfy the one who suffered it by the other's penalty." "Then the one who inflicts injury would seem to you more wretched than the one who receives it." "So then," said she, "the one who did wrong would seem to you more wretched than the one who endured it." "It follows," I said. "It comes to that," said I. "From this, then, and for other reasons

resting on that root, that baseness by its own nature makes people wretched, it is clear that an injury inflicted on anyone is the wretchedness not of the one who receives it but of the one who inflicts it. "So," I said again, "from that argument, and from other arguments also rooted in the same way, that a shameful deed by itself makes people wretched, what you say also becomes clear: that the wretchedness belongs to the one who does the wrong, not to the one who suffers it." That is an argument from the efficient cause. Baseness is the efficient cause of the wretched, just as, conversely, honour, that is, virtue, is that of the blessed. Baseness is the common name of all vices, just as honour is of all virtues.

"WHOEVER IS MORE WRETCHED, HE RATHER" — "And yet now," she said, "the orators do the opposite." Advocates now act against this, she said — "OUGHT TO BE PITIED." For they try to stir up the pity of the judges for those who have suffered something grievous and bitter. They keep urging the judges to have pity on those to whom much harm has been done. Yet a juster pity is owed rather to those who commit the wrong. In fact the wrongdoers would be in greater need of pity.
These people ought to be brought to judgment like the sick to a physician, not by angry accusers but rather by kindly and compassionate ones,

so that they might cut away the diseases of guilt by punishment. Their accusers ought to bring them to court the way one brings the sick to a physician: not out of hatred, but out of mercy and compassion, so that they might do them good there by cutting out the gall of their sins. That is an argument from likeness (argumentum a simili). For just as the body needs medicine, so also does the soul. In this way the whole work of defenders would grow cold. Or, if they preferred to help people, it would be turned into the form, that is, the manner, of accusation. In that case the efforts of the advocates would be given up. Or, if they wished to help anyone, they would do it by accusing him instead of defending him.

The wicked themselves too, if they were allowed to glimpse through some small crack the virtue they had abandoned, and saw that they would put off the filth of their vices through the torments of punishment,

in exchange for the goodness they would gain, would not count these torments as torments. If the wicked themselves could look out at all at the virtue they have cast away, even as if through a crack, and saw that they would be washed clean of their sins by the severity of the punishment, in return for gaining goodness, would they then count it as punishment? They would also reject the work of their defenders and give themselves over entirely to their accusers and judges.

They would not ask for the help of advocates. Instead they would give themselves over to their accusers and also to the judges, so that these might chastise them. So it comes about that among the wise no place at all is left for hatred. If they act in this way, there is no path that could lead the wise to hatred. For who but the greatest fool would hate the good? And to hate the wicked makes no sense. As you can see from these arguments: Who would hate the good, except the worst of creatures? That is an argument from contraries (argumentum a contrariis), for the foolish and malicious are the opposite of the good. And that anyone should hate the wicked, what sense is there in that? That is an argument from incompatibles (a repugnantibus), for unjust hatred is incompatible with reason.
For if viciousness is a kind of disease of souls, just as sickness is of bodies, and since we judge that those who are sick in body by no means deserve hatred,

but rather with pity; much more are they not to be pursued (that is, with death) but to be pitied, whose minds are oppressed by wickedness, which is more savage than any sickness. If lack of virtue is a sickness of the mind, just as corruption of the body is the body's sickness, and those who are sick in their bodies do not seem to us to deserve hatred but pity, then those whose minds are stifled by wickedness, the most grievous of all diseases, are not to be persecuted; rather, pity is to be had on them.
WHY WOULD ANYONE KILL THOSE WHO ARE GOING TO DIE OF THEIR OWN ACCORD? What good is it to stir up such great commotions and to provoke
fate with your own hand? Why do you desire to show such great wrath, and to bring on death with your hand?
If you seek death, it draws near of its own accord!
nor does it hold back its swift horses.
If you desire it, it comes uninvited, of its own will, and it does not delay its journey. Those whom the serpent, the lion, the tiger, the bear, the boar
attack with their teeth, these same people nevertheless attack themselves with the sword. Those whom all the animals pursue slay themselves needlessly on top of that with weapons.
Or is it because their ways differ and disagree
that they set unjust battle lines and savage wars in motion,
and wish to perish by each other's weapons?

That is not a just enough reason for cruelty. Because their customs differ and do not agree, do they draw up troops against each other over that, and fight over that? That is no just reason at all for such severity!
Do you wish to give deserts a fitting return?
Love the good, as is right, and have pity on the bad. Do you wish to reward each person according to his deserts? Then do this: love the good, as is right, and have mercy on the wicked.
WHY THINGS ARE MIXED AS IF BY CHANCE EVENTS, SO THAT EVILS COME TO THE GOOD AND GOODS TO THE BAD. Here I said: Then I said: I see what happiness
or misery [heading continues: BEFALL] is established in the very deserts of the upright and of the wicked,
but I judge that there is some good or evil in this common fortune itself.

I see well what happiness or what misery lies in the deserts of both of them, the good and the bad. Yet I also find in the people's fortunes themselves that there is good and evil. For none of the wise would rather be an exile, poor and disgraced, than flourish, staying in his own city, strong in wealth, revered in honour, mighty in power. That is clear from the choice of the wise: none of them is as glad to be in exile, poor and despised, as he is glad to be at home, rich, honoured and mighty,

and well provided in all things. For in this way the office of wisdom is carried out more clearly and with more evidence, when the happiness of the rulers is in some way passed on to the peoples who come under them. In this way they carry out the office of their wisdom more visibly and with better testimony, if their happiness, while they are to govern the people, becomes known even among outsiders. This is especially so since prison, law, and the other torments of legal punishment are owed rather to harmful citizens,
for whose sake they were also established. Why, then, are these things turned the other way around, so that the punishments for crimes weigh on the good, and the wicked seize the rewards of virtue?

I wonder greatly. And how perils such as these, prisons, law-books, and all the punishments devised according to the law ought to harm those for whose sake they were established: why there should be such a reversal, so that suffering oppresses the good instead of the wicked, and the wicked snatch away the honor of the good, at this I wonder greatly. And I desire to learn from you what the reason for such unjust confusion seems to be. And I would gladly learn from you what the reason for such unjust mixing-up is. For I would wonder less if I believed that all things were mixed up by chance events. I would not wonder at it at all if I believed that all things were truly tossed about in uncertain happenings.
Now God the ruler heaps up my astonishment.

Since he often grants pleasant things to the good and harsh things to the wicked, and on the other hand gives hard things to the good and grants the wicked what they desire, then unless the cause is discovered, what is there that would seem to make this differ from chance events? God the ruler makes my astonishment great. Since he is so disposed that he often gives joy to the good and hardship to the wicked, and again, on the contrary, hardship to the good and pleasure to the wicked, and I find no reason for it, how then should it seem to me to be distinguished from fickle happenings? "It is no wonder," she said, "if something whose principle of order is unknown is believed to be random and confused." "No wonder," she said, "if people think that thing is disorderly and confused when no reason for its order has been learned."

"But although you do not know the cause of so great an arrangement, do not doubt that all things are done rightly, since a good ruler governs the world." "But even though you do not know what the purpose of such a mighty reckoning is, still, since the one who measures out the world is a good ruler, do not doubt it: everything is rightly ordered. For it must be that the righteous one acts rightly." These two words are paired. That is why this is called an argument from conjugates (argumentum a coniugatis).
THINGS WHOSE REASON IS NOT KNOWN RIGHTLY SEEM WONDROUS.
If anyone does not know that the stars of Arcturus, that is, the star called Arcturus,
glide close to the highest pole, and if anyone does not know why
slow Bootes leads, that is, follows, the Wagon, slow, that is, slow to set,
and plunges his late flames into the sea,
while he unfolds his risings all too swiftly,
he will be astonished at the law of the high heaven.

Whoever does not know [what] stands here near the north pole of heaven, and why the constellation of Bootes, in which Arcturus stands, slowly follows the Wagon, goes slowly to its setting, and yet rises quickly, must necessarily wonder how this comes about up above us in heaven. Because the north pole is above the earth, just as the south pole is below the earth, the signs that hover nearest to it do not set, as the Arcti do, which people call the Wagon. Those that stand somewhat farther off, as Bootes does, set for a while, so that they make a short journey under the earth compared with the one they make above the earth. Whoever does not know this may well wonder at it. Duae arcti, that is, duae ursae (the two Bears).

...Helix and Cynosura. Helix is the name of the greater one [the Great Bear]. On it one sees seven bright stars, which are called Septentrio. Boötes follows it, because he goes behind it, and wherever it turns its hind parts, there one sees Boötes. Why the horns of the full moon grow pale, tinged (that is, darkened) by the limits of the dark night (that is, by its nightly courses), and why Phoebe, confounded (that is, obscured), uncovers the stars (that is, by failing)
which she had covered with her shining face.

It may also be a wonder to them why the full moon, when an eclipse of the moon happens in the middle of the night, suddenly grows altogether dark and lets the lesser stars shine, which it covered before, as long as it had to shine brightly. It is plain that the moon has no light of its own, and that the sun makes it bright by shining on it, and that it is always moving either away from the sun or toward the sun. Therefore it happens that when, at full moon, it goes so far that it stands directly opposite the sun on the other side of the heaven, and the earth is between them, its light fails it in that place, until it moves further on, to where the sun can shine on it. That failing is called an eclipse of the moon.
The public error (that is, the common error) stirs up the peoples. Then the people are alarmed at something about which they are all in error. They wonder what it means.
And they weary the air with frequent beatings (that is, with people asking). And then they keep asking about it, until the heaven itself may grow weary of their asking.
No one marvels at the blasts of Corus [the northwest wind]
beating the shore with roaring wave. But on the other hand no one marvels at it when the wind blows and the wave strikes the shore.
Nor that the mass of snow, hard with cold,
is loosened by the burning heat of Phoebus. Nor that the ice melts from the heat of the sun. Why is that?
For here it is easy to discern the causes. Because these causes are easy to understand.
There hidden ones (that is, causes) trouble hearts. But those causes are hard to understand, because they hide themselves.
Everything that a rare age brings forth. Everything that happens rarely.
And the fickle crowd is astonished at sudden things. And at which the common people are alarmed when it happens suddenly. Let it yield to ignorance
that is, if the clouded error of ignorance should yield. If they are instructed about it,
they assuredly cease to seem wondrous.
Then there is at once an end to the wondering. It is so, I said. It is so, said I.
THE PETITION, AND HOW DIFFICULT THE THINGS ASKED FOR ARE TO GRANT. But since it is your office to unfold the causes of hidden things and to explain reasons veiled in darkness,
I beg you to judge this matter and explain it, since this marvel disturbs me most of all. But since it is your task alone to tell

what all things each mean, and to explain secret reasoning, why that is which I asked about, I beg you to tell me and instruct me about it, because so heavy a wonder seizes me over it. Then she, smiling a little, said: You summon me to the greatest of all matters to be asked about, for which scarcely anything exhaustive is enough. She then, laughing a little at me, said: Now you are directing me to the greatest of all questions, for which no answer is ever enough.

"For such is the nature of this matter that when one doubt is cut away, countless others grow up in its place, like the heads of the Hydra." Its nature is such to answer, and it is the kind of thing in which, when one doubt is removed, many come up in its place. This is what happened to Hercules when he had to slay the serpent that is called hydra in Greek and excedra in Latin. When he struck off one of its heads, three grew in its place, and from those that were struck off, many more. "Nor would there be any limit to them, unless someone held them in check with the most living fire of the mind." There will be no end to them unless they are subdued with the lively fire of the mind. This is what Hercules did to the Lernaean marsh, from which this fable arose. Because he could not dam it up and block it, and it kept breaking out, he attacked it with fire, and with that fire he dried it up [?]. "For in this ..."

"... (namely, in this matter) people usually ask about the simplicity of providence." Here we must ask about God's simple providence. It is simple and single, and unlike human providence. It sees everything together, at a single glance. A human being sees only some things, and sees even those one at a time, as she teaches later in the fifth book. For this reason human providence is what we call forethought and precaution. But God's providence is an oversight that takes in everything at once. It is not divided by times and places, and through it the present,

the past and the future, the higher and the lower, are all grasped together. But because his providentia is sometimes used in place of praescientia, it is also rendered as foreknowledge or foresight. This is not its proper sense. It follows the pattern of human foresight and foreknowing. With God, all of it is a looking-upon and an overseeing. "About the chain of fate": about the onward sequence of God's will. "About sudden chance events": about sudden happenings. "About divine knowledge and predestination": about God's knowing and appointing. "About freedom of choice": about self-choice. Here it should be understood that, for convenience, we translate liberum arbitrium as "selbwala" (self-choice),

as if it meant liberam electionem (free choice). But Boethius teaches us in the third book of the second edition of his commentary on the Peri Hermeneias that we should say liberum arbitrium with the word voluntatis understood, that is, liberum voluntatis arbitrium (free choice of the will). God has made us arbiters and judges of our own wills, whether they are good or evil. That is why it says liberum voluntatis arbitrium, the self-governing choosing of the will. But if we say that liberum arbitrium means libera voluntas (free will), we aim at the same thing, and we then have three words captured in two. We ought to render those two as "willewaltigi" (power over one's own will), except that in our language this word has the meaning that liberalitas has among the Latins. So Terence says: "serviebas liberaliter" (you served as a free man would). We put it this way: "You served willingly." "How heavy these matters are, you weigh for yourself." How heavy that is, you know.

But since knowing these things is also part of your cure, we will nevertheless try to settle (that is, define) something, although we are hemmed in by a narrow limit (that is, path) of time. But because this also bears on your cure, if you are to understand it, I shall nevertheless manage [?] to speak of it, though there is too little time for it before the end of this book.
But if the delights of music (that is, of metrical song) please you, you must put off this pleasure for a little while, until I weave together in order

the arguments that are linked to one another. If you desire metrical song, wait for it a while, until I weave for you, in order, the arguments that hold together. "As you wish," I said. "As you wish," I said. Then, as if starting from another beginning, she spoke as follows. She then, as if setting out on another path, spoke thus.

ON PROVIDENCE AND FATE. [It obtains] its forms (that is, what kind of thing it is) from the stability of the divine mind. The generation of all things (that is, of living things), and the whole progress of changeable natures (as the seasons are), and whatever is moved in any way (the sun and the moon), [obtain] their causes (that is, why it is),

[and their] order (that is, how it is). The birth of all things, and the course of all changeable things, and everything that moves in any way, has all of this from the steadfastness of God's wisdom: why it is, how it is, and of what kind it is. This (that is, the stability), set (that is, placed) in the citadel (that is, the dignity) of its simplicity, establishes a manifold way of governing things. It sits in its majesty, simple in itself, and directs other things in manifold ways.
When this way is beheld in the very purity of the divine intelligence, it is called providence;

but when it is related to the things it moves and orders, the ancients called it fate. This same way has two names. The first applies when one thinks of it in the pure wisdom of God himself: then the way is called providentia. The second applies when one looks at the things that it drives and orders: then it is called fatum in the old writings. In the same way, our own work also has two modes: one, in which it exists all together in the mind, disposing (disponens); the other, in which it is carried out piece by piece with the hands, effecting (efficiens). That these two are different will easily become clear if anyone considers the force of each in his mind. Whoever considers them both will easily see that they are distinct.
For providence is that very divine reason, established in the highest ruler of all,

which orders all things. For providence is the very rationality that resides in God, which establishes each and every thing. But fate is the ordering inherent in changeable things, through which providence binds each thing into its own order. But fate is the very ordering attached to all changeable things, by which providence constrains each thing into its order. For providence embraces all things together, however diverse, however infinite they are. Providence embraces all things together, however varied they may be and however endless they may be.
But fate arranges individual things in motion, distributed in places, forms, and times. Fate directs them one by one in their course, distributed here and there.

[?] in such and such ways, at those times, and in those [?]. So that this unfolding of the temporal order, united in the foresight of the divine mind, is providence; but the same unity, distributed and unfolded in time, is called fate. In this way: the ordering that follows the order of time, uniting itself in the foresight of God's mind, is called providentia; and when it is unfolded instead at separate times [?]

it is called fatum. Although these are different, one still depends on the other. For the order of fate proceeds from the simplicity of providence. Although the two are not one, still the one hangs on the other, because fate comes from providence.
For just as a craftsman, grasping in his mind the form of the thing to be made, sets the work in motion, and what he had foreseen simply and as present to him,

he carries out through the orders of time, so God's providence disposes, singly and stably, the things that are to be done, but through fate it administers these very things it has disposed in many ways and in time. Just as the carpenter first shapes in his mind what he means to do, and afterwards works it; and what he conceived in the unified presence of his mind, he carries out piece by piece: so it happens that God's providence, in steadfast oneness, determines what is to be done, and afterwards he accomplishes it through fate in manifold ways and in due order. Whether, then, fate is carried out
by certain divine spirits serving providence, or by the soul, or by the whole of nature serving it, or by the heavenly motions of the stars, or by the power of angels,
or by the varied cunning of demons, or whether the chain of fate is woven by some of these or by all of them, this at least is clear: that providence is the unmoving form of the things to be done,
and simple; but fate is the moving bond and temporal order of those things that the divine simplicity has disposed to be done. Whether fate is accomplished

by God's own sevenfold Spirit serving providence, or by the soul serving it, or by both soul and body, or by the sun and moon, or by angels, or by the devil's cunning, or by some of these serving, or even by all of them serving, and the course of fate is guided by them, this much is always certain: that providence is the still and single shaping of the things that are to happen, but fate is the moving bond and temporal ordering of those things that God's simplicity shaped to be done.
SPIRITUAL CREATURES ARE SUBJECT TO PROVIDENCE, BODILY CREATURES TO FATE. From this it follows that all things that are under fate are also subject to providence, to which fate itself is also subject.

But some things which are placed under providence surpass the chain of fate. For this reason it is so arranged that the things subject to fate are subject to providence, to which fate itself is also subject. And yet some things subject to providence rise above fate. These are the things which, firmly fixed close to the first divinity, go beyond the order of fate's changeableness. Those are the things which, set firm together with God, do not suffer the orders of running fate, because they are near to him. Those things are subject to providence which are steadfast in their nature, but those things are subject to fate which are driven by it. So fate too is subject to providence, because providence comes first, in God's will, and fate follows that will and carries it out.

For just as, of the circles turning around the same pivot, the one that is innermost comes close to the simplicity of the centre (Suspension of the voice.) Just as, of the many rings that turn on the wheel around one axle-pin, the one that is innermost of all is nearest to the pin. and is, for the others placed outside it, a kind of pivot around which they turn. (And here.) And it too, for the others running outside around it, because of its nearness to the pin,
is itself like a pin. But the outermost, turned with a wider circuit, is spread out over wider spaces the further it moves away from the indivisible centre point.

(And here.) But the outermost, having a greater sweep, spreads itself out the wider, the farther it is from the narrowness of the point there in the middle. But whatever joins and attaches itself to that centre is drawn together into simplicity, and stops spreading and flowing apart. (And here.) But whatever holds itself to the middle draws itself together, unspread and undispersed. By the same reasoning, whatever moves further away from the first mind is entangled in greater bonds of fate, and a thing is freer from fate the nearer it comes to that pivot of things. (Lowering of the voice.) In the same way, whatever has moved far from the will that comes first, that is, God's providence, is bound with more bonds of fate. And each thing is so much more free

of fate, the nearer it has moved to the innermost hinge. If you ask what those bonds and fetters and knots are: they are the causes of all things, and the very things whose causes they are hold fast to them. This is how it goes when God's wrath comes about because of sins, and from that comes intemperate weather, and from intemperate weather come diseases, and from diseases death. Each of these holds to the next. But if it clings to the firmness of the mind on high, it is without motion and also rises above the necessity of fate. If it also holds closely to the firmness of God's providence, then it is free of change, and so it is without the necessity of fate. The things that suffer change are earthly. But what changes do heavenly things suffer? The heavenly messengers also travel from place to place.

which they nevertheless do non-locally (inlocaliter). For they do not have before and behind, right and left, above and below, as bodily things have. Inwardly they are always unchanged in the presence of God. But those who are so inwardly with God that they do not change their place and do not carry messages, as the scriptures say of the cherubim and seraphim, what change can we say that they undergo? Therefore, as reasoning is to understanding, as that which is begotten is to that which is, as time is to eternity, as the circle is to the center point, so is the moving series of fate to the stable simplicity of providence. Fate has the same relation to providence that reasoning (ratiocinatio) has to understanding (intellectus). When we infer one thing from another,

as Aristotle taught, that is reasoning (ratiocinatio). Human wisdom has discovered these methods. They will be made void (euacuati) when the eyes of men are opened in a heavenly way and their mind is drawn upward to know what no philosophical reasoning knows. In that lies understanding (intellectus). Thus we know that God is above all things, and that he is in the world in such a way that he contains it, not it him. He is in it in such a way that he is not enclosed in it. Human reason does not know how this can be; divine understanding teaches it. That question will come to us again in the fifth book. Fate is also to providence as that which becomes is to that which is. That which becomes also passes away, and it changes for as long as it lasts.

Or, if it is not to pass away, then it is changeable until God makes it unchangeable, as he did with the good angels at the fall of the wicked ones. But God, who is, is imperishable and unchangeable. Fate is also to providence as time is to eternity. Time runs through three tenses: present, past and future. Eternity always stays fixed in the present. And it is as the circle is to the point that stands in its middle. The circle has its course around, and its measure and its width; the point has no size at all. Therefore it is without measure and without parts. It is an indivisible thing.
WHAT FATE CAN DO.

That series moves the heaven and the stars. The ordered course of that same fate turns the heaven around together with the stars. The ancients, as Servius says, called fate vox Iovis, 'the voice of Jupiter', as if whatever was to happen to each man was what Jupiter had decreed for him by speaking. That is why many people explain fatum as 'urlag' [fate, destiny]. But since God's will is to be carried out in certain events, and the inner ordaining is to be made manifest in his outward ordaining, that outward ordaining is called fatum, as was also said before, just as the inner one is called providentia. The sequence that lies in it, and its ordering from beginning to end, is called series, from serendo ['sowing'], after the sowing of the farmer, who sows onward along the length of the furrow

until he has gone through it. It tempers the elements with one another and transforms them by alternating change. It moderates the elements among themselves and brings them into harmony, although they are contrary to one another, and gives them forms that change into each other in turn. For men who have come from earth become earth again, and then men again; but birds that have come from water do not become water again, but earth. The same renews all things that are born and that perish, through similar progressions of offspring and seeds. That same order of fate, that is, of God's outward ordaining, renews and replaces all changeable things, which at one time come into being and at another pass away, by a like increase of their seed and of their offspring. This also constrains the deeds

and fortunes of men by an indissoluble chain of causes. This also constrains the deeds of men and their fortune with the firm bond of causes. Nothing happens by chance; it always happens from some source, as death comes from sickness or from wounds. That from which it happens is its cause; that is its seed; that is its making; that is its ordering, which binds it firmly to itself. Since this proceeds from the beginnings of immovable providence, it must also be unchangeable itself. That order must of necessity be unchangeable, because it comes from there, from the steadfast providentia. For thus things are best governed.
if the simplicity abiding in the divine mind puts forth an unswerving order of causes.

Thus God arranges it all best, if the simplicity of his mind gives an unchangeable order to the seeds that direct each thing. But this order should restrain changeable things by its own unchangeableness, things that would otherwise drift about at random. This outer order, which comes from the inner one, must constrain the changeable things with its unchangeableness, things that would otherwise waver about wrongly. Hence it happens that, although to you, who are quite unable to consider this order, all things seem confused and disturbed, nevertheless its own measure, directing toward the good, disposes all things. From this it follows that, however much all things seem confused and erring to you who do not recognize this order, his way, aiming at the good, directs all things no less for that.
For there is nothing that is done for the sake of evil, not even by the wicked themselves, whom perverse error has turned aside while they were seeking the good.

as has been most abundantly shown; much less would the order proceeding from the hinge of the highest good turn aside in any way from its beginning. No one does anything for the sake of evil, not even the evil themselves, who are striving toward the good when error turns them aside, as I have said sufficiently. How then should an order that comes from God move in any other way than after him?
THAT FROM THE HIDDEN DEPTHS OF PROVIDENCE ARE DISPENSED THE THINGS THAT SUIT THE GOOD AND THE WICKED, AND THAT MEN WONDER AT THIS. "But what confusion," you will say, "can be more unjust

than that the good meet now with adversity, now with prosperity, and the wicked likewise now with what they desire, now with what they hate?" So you say: what lack of distinction can be more unjust than that pleasant and painful things befall the good and the evil alike?
Do men, then, live with such soundness of mind that those whom they have judged good

or bad must necessarily also be as they think? Are people, then, of such sound mind that those whom they consider good or bad must necessarily be as they consider them? And yet in this the judgments of men conflict, and those whom some think worthy of reward, others think worthy of punishment. Truly, people always disagree about this: those who seem to some to deserve good seem to others to deserve evil. But let us grant that someone could tell the good from the bad. Now let us nevertheless say that someone could discern who is good
or bad. Will he then be able to see into that inmost temperament, that is, the mixture, of souls, as is usually said of bodies

namely by physicians? Can he also know the inner nature of the mind, as physicians say of bodies that they know it? For it is no different a marvel to someone who does not know why, among healthy bodies, sweet things suit some and bitter things suit others, and why, among the sick, some are helped by gentle remedies and others by sharp ones. It may seem just as great a wonder to someone who does not know it why, among healthy bodies, sweet things agree with some and bitter things with others; and why some sick people are healed with sour things and others with mild ones.
But the physician, who discerns the measure and temperament

of health itself and of sickness, is not at all surprised at this. But the physician who recognizes the measure and the tempering of sickness and of health is not struck by any wonder at it. And what else does the health of souls seem to be but goodness? What else is their sickness but vice? What else can the mind's health be but goodness? And what is its sickness but vices? And who else preserves the good and drives away the bad but God, the ruler and healer of minds? Who is it, too, that keeps good within and drives evil out, except God, the ruler and physician of human minds?
When he has looked out from the high watchtower of providence, he recognizes what suits each one, and he assigns what he knows to be suitable.

When he looks down here from the watchtower of his providence and perceives what befits each one, he then gives him what he recognizes to befit him. Here now occurs that remarkable wonder of the order of fate, when one who knows does what astonishes those who do not know. So then comes about the singular wonder of fate proceeding in rightness: that God knowingly does what startles the unknowing.

THAT MEN AND PROVIDENCE DO NOT JUDGE ALIKE. For, to touch briefly on a few things about the divine depth that human reason is able to grasp: concerning this man whom you think most just and most careful to observe what is fair,

…seems otherwise to the all-knowing providence. So that I may still give you some grounding in the divine matter, as much as a man is capable of: the one you consider most just and most equitable of all seems otherwise to the all-knowing providence. And indeed our friend Lucan reminded us that the victorious cause pleased the gods, but the vanquished one pleased Cato. And that is what my dear Lucan told you: that the cause that won the victory pleased the gods, but the cause that lost pleased Cato. If Caesar's cause had not pleased them, they would not have helped him to victory! And if Pompey's cause, even without victory, had not pleased Cato well, it would not have seemed better to him to kill himself than to surrender to Caesar.
Here, therefore, whatever you see happen contrary to your hope, there is indeed right order in the things themselves, but a perverse confusion in your opinion.

Know, therefore, that whatever you see happen here in the world contrary to your hope is all right ordering for the things themselves, but wrong confusion for your opinion. With this she has answered his question, though she will still show him the same thing point by point.

THE VARIETY OF DISPENSATION TOWARD THE GOOD. But suppose someone is so well-mannered that divine and human judgment agree about him alike. Now suppose there is someone so upright in conduct that God and man value him alike. But he is weak in strength of mind. He may happen to be soft-hearted.

If anything adverse befalls him, he will perhaps stop cultivating the innocence through which he could not keep his fortune. If anything grievous befalls him, he will perhaps stop holding fast to righteousness, since it brought him no good fortune.
Therefore wise dispensation spares the one whom adversity could make worse,

so that it does not let anyone suffer hardship who is not suited to it. God's measuring spares him and does not thrust him into hardship, because it does not suit him and would make him worse. Another is perfect in all virtues, holy and closest to God.
Providence judges it wrong for him to be touched by any adversities at all, so much so that it does not let him be troubled even by bodily illnesses. Likewise, someone is full of all virtues,

holy and godly. God judges him unworthy of any trouble, so much so that he does not even let him become sick. For, as someone more excellent than I said, virtues have built (that is, fortified) the body of a holy man: andros de ieras daumasa aliteres icodomeson [? garbled Greek]. For, as someone wiser than I said, virtues have so fortified the body of a holy man that nothing can harm it. She says "wiser." Who can be wiser than Wisdom herself? Yet by speaking this way she teaches us humility.
It also often happens that the supreme government of affairs is handed over to the good,
so that overflowing wickedness may be beaten back.

It also often happens that power comes into the hands of the good, so that the evil that has grown up may be suppressed by them. To others it distributes certain mixed things according to the quality of their minds. To some, God lets both kinds of things happen, the toilsome and the pleasant, according to the nature of their minds. Some it bites back, lest they grow wanton through long happiness. Some he chastises from time to time, so that they do not become arrogant from long prosperity.
He lets others be tossed by hardships, so that they may strengthen the virtues of the mind through the practice of patience

and through exercise. He wants some to be tested with hardships so that they may gain virtuous minds by hardening themselves and growing used to patience. Some fear more than is right what they are able to bear; others despise more than is right what they are not able to bear. These he leads through sorrows to a test of themselves. Some are needlessly frightened of what they could well endure; others trust themselves too far. He brings both into distress so that they may come to know themselves. Some have bought a name honoured in the world at the price of a glorious death. Some have been able to win a famous name in the world through a brave death, like Judas Maccabeus. Some, that is, like the martyrs,

unconquerable under tortures, have set an example to the rest that virtue cannot be conquered by evils. Some, tortured for the sake of righteousness and unconquered in it, gave others an example of this: that true virtue is not overcome by torments. How rightly and in what good order these things are done,

and for the good of those to whom they seem to happen, there is no doubt. How rightly and how orderly all these things happen is also certain from the very blessedness of those to whom they have happened.

HOW THE WICKED TOO ARE VARIOUSLY DEALT WITH. For this too, that the wicked meet now with sorrowful things and now with things they desire, comes from the same causes. That both sorrow and joy also happen to the wicked comes from the same source, divine providence.
And no one wonders at the sorrowful things, because everyone thinks they deserve ill. No one wonders that sorrow happens to them, because everyone thinks they deserve evil.
Their punishments both deter others from crimes and correct the very people on whom they are inflicted. Their punishment does two good things.

It turns others away from guilt, and those on whom it is inflicted it draws away from guilt. But the joyful things give the good a strong proof of what they ought to think of this kind of happiness, which they often see serving the wicked. But the fact that pleasant things befall the wicked teaches the good thoroughly what they should take that happiness to be, which comes even to the wicked.
In this matter I believe this is also arranged: that perhaps someone's nature is so headlong and so unruly
that poverty in household goods could instead drive him into crimes.

In this I also believe that God intends this: that some person's nature is so rash and so restless that he would ruin himself because of poverty in goods. Providence heals this man's disease with the remedy of money given to him. Providence calms his wickedness with the reward of treasure. This man, seeing his conscience stained with disgraceful deeds and comparing himself with his fortune, perhaps becomes afraid that losing what he enjoys using would be painful.
So he will change his ways, and while he fears to lose his fortune,

...abandons wickedness. A certain man recognizes how he has acted, and when he measures his good fortune against that, he is afraid that he may lose such joy, lest it then go hard with him [?]. So he changes his life and, fearing misfortune, gives up wickedness. Others an undeservedly increased good fortune has thrown headlong into deserved ruin. For some it turned out that their unjustly won good fortune hurled them into the ruin they deserved. To some the right of punishing has been permitted, so that it might be a cause of training for the good and of punishment for the wicked. To some power was granted to torment people: for the good as a hardening trial, for the wicked as retribution.
For just as there is no bond between the upright and the wicked,

so the wicked themselves cannot agree among themselves. You need not wonder at all that one wicked man torments another. For just as there is no common mind between the good and the wicked, so there is not full concord among the wicked themselves either. Why not, since each disagrees with himself, while his vices tear his conscience apart? How could it be otherwise, since each of them strives even with himself, his conscience torn apart by his vices? And they often do things that, once done, they judge should not have been done. And they often do what their conscience tells them is not to be done! Yet they do it. When their conscience grieves them, they strive with themselves.
From this that highest providence has often brought forth a remarkable miracle: that bad men made bad men good.

From this God's providence has often brought forth that singular sign: that bad men make good men out of bad ones. For when some see themselves suffering injustice from the worst men, they burn with hatred of the guilty and return to the fruit of virtue, while they strive to be unlike those whom they hated. That is the wonder I speak of. When unrighteous men see that they are made to suffer by other unrighteous men, they conceive hatred for them and turn to goodness, hastening to be unlike those whom they hate.
THAT THERE IS NO EVIL ANYWHERE. For it is the divine power alone

to which even evils are good, since by using them fittingly it draws out the effect of some good. The power of the one God is such that even evil is good to him, because by using it fittingly he turns it to good. For a certain order embraces all things,

so that whatever departs from the assigned, that is, the fixed, plan of the order falls back into it, even if into another order, so that nothing in the realm of providence may be left to random chance.

The order of God's providence encompasses all things. If any thing swerves from the sure direction of its order, it is at once turned into another order, so that nothing in God's kingdom is ever allowed to be disordered. Whatever will not keep to its right way is nevertheless always brought back onto the way. The envy of Joseph's eleven brothers, in which they had abandoned the right way, God brought back onto the way when, by occasion of that very envy, he raised Joseph above them and humbled them before the one they thought they had crushed. Most mighty God in the world: Argalthon demetauta theonos [?] (garbled Greek); he accomplished all things; panta gopiin [?] (garbled Greek). The mighty God has always done in the world all that he wished.
For it is not permitted to man either to grasp with his mind or to set forth in speech all the workings of the divine work. Nor is it granted to men to know or to tell all of God's arrangements.

Let it be enough to have seen only this: that God, the producer (that is, the bringer-forth) of all natures, likewise directing them to the good, disposes all things. Only let this be well understood:

that God, the creator of all natures, orders all things, always turning them toward good. And while he hastens to keep the things he brought forth in his own likeness, he banishes all evil from the bounds of his commonwealth through the chain of fated necessity. And by compelling the things he created toward his likeness, he drives every evil out of his kingdom through the necessary ordering of fate, because he wills that the things that come from the good should be good. Hence it comes about
that if you look at the providence that orders all things, you will judge that there is nothing evil anywhere,

…that is, of the evils which are believed to abound on earth. It follows that if you look to God's ordering, you will consider that there is nowhere anything of any evil, though people think the world is full of it. But I see that you have long been both burdened by the weight of the question and wearied by the length of the reasoning, and are waiting for some sweetness of song. Now I see, then, that because of the heaviness of this laborious question and the toil of the long answer, you long once more for sweet song. Take therefore a draught, so that, refreshed by it,
you may press on more firmly to what lies further. Now drink what I give you, so that with this refreshment you may move on further.
That by God's providence all things are bound together by love, so that they are not dissolved.
If you wish, with skill and with a pure mind, to discern the laws of the Thunderer on high,
look at the heights of the highest heaven. There the stars keep their ancient peace
by the just covenant of things. If you wish to know thoroughly how firm God's law is, then look into heaven.
There the stars still firmly keep the harmony that they have always kept according to their ordering.
The sun, driven onward with its ruddy fire, does not
hinder the cold axle of Phoebe. As is evident there, the hot sun does not hinder the cold moon in its course.
Nor does the Bear, which turns its swift courses at the highest summit of the world,
seeing the other stars sink into the western ocean,
ever desire to dip its flames, washing them in the deep. Nor does Helice, which turns very swiftly around the gable of heaven,
though it sees all the signs going down to their setting, ever desire to bathe itself in the water of the sea.
Vesper announces the late shadows,
and Lucifer always brings back the kindly day, in equal turns of time. The evening star always announces the night, and in answer the morning star brings us the day just as many times.
So mutual love renews the eternal courses;
so discordant war is banished from the star-bearing regions. So love in alternation renews the untiring courses, and quarrelsome discord flees from heaven.
This concord tempers the warring elements in equal measures. This concord unites the opposing elements in like ways,
so that wet things yield in turn to dry,
and cold things keep faith with flames;
the hovering fire rises on high,

and heavy things sink down by the weight of the earth. In this way they are balanced: the dry agrees with the wet, and the cold with the hot, and the light fire presses up to the very top, and the heavy earth sinks to the very bottom.
For these reasons the flowering year breathes out its scents in the warm spring.
Burning summer dries the grain.
Autumn returns heavy with fruit.

Falling rain waters the winter. From this comes the scent of the flowers at the time of year when it is spring. From this the grain ripens in summertime. Autumn comes laden with fruit, and winter wet with rain.
This tempering nourishes and brings forth
whatever breathes life in the world. This moderation gives life to and nourishes whatever is living anywhere in the world.
The same, snatching away,
hides and takes away what has come into being, sinking it in final death. And again, as it changes, it gives and it takes all things that have come into being, sinking them into death.
Meanwhile the Creator sits on high
and, ruling, guides the reins of things,
king and lord, fountain and origin,

law and wise judge of what is just. Meanwhile the Creator sits above, and, ruling, he turns the bridle of the world: lord and king, beginning and source, the law itself, and wise judge of what is right.
And the things he stirs by motion to go,

he draws back and halts, and he makes firm the things that wander. And the things he sets moving on their way, he steadies by drawing the bridle toward himself, and he turns their course, for he forces them back toward himself.
For unless, calling back their straight paths,
he forced them again into curving orbits,
the things that a stable order now holds together

would be cut off from their source and fall apart. If he did not do this, and did not bend back into a circle the courses that run straight away, then the things that a sure order now holds fast would fly apart and be cut off from their origin.

This is the love common to all things. This is the love I am speaking of, which is common to all things. God himself is what they love, for he is the highest good (summum bonum), and they came from him.
And they seek again, that is, they desire, to be held by the end of the good. And so they long to be bound to the end of the good, which he is.
Because they could not last in any other way
unless, with their love turned back, they flowed back to the cause, that is, unless they joined themselves to that cause

which gave them being. For they could not exist in any other way unless they made their way back, with their love turned around, to the God who commanded them to come into being, who is the cause of them all.
THAT ALL FORTUNE IS GOOD. So do you see now what follows from all these things we have said?

"Do you not now perceive what necessarily follows from all these things?" "What then?" I said. "What, I said?" "That all fortune is entirely good," she said. "That both are good: good fortune and misfortune."
